articles.title: Volunteers brave rain to help Rochdale Sea Cadets at Hollingworth Lake
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Sea Cadets have thanked Get Together After Serving CIC after volunteers spent a wet morning clearing overgrowth around their boat shed at Hollingworth Lake.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Sea Cadets have thanked volunteers from Get Together After Serving CIC after they spent a wet morning clearing overgrowth around the unit’s boat shed at Hollingworth Lake.

The cadets shared their appreciation for the team’s efforts, saying: “We are so grateful to you for your help, you have done an amazing job.”

The clearance is a practical example of local groups supporting one another, with volunteers giving their time despite the rain.

articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: The house on Clegg Hall Road is real and well documented; the boggart belongs to Lancashire folklore, not to the record office.
articles.summary: The house on Clegg Hall Road is real and well documented; the boggart belongs to Lancashire folklore, not to the record office.
articles.body:
Short answer up front: the house, its date and fabric are documented; the murder tale and the angry spirit are part of oral and printed folklore rather than verified history.

Clegg Hall stands where the lane named for it climbs from the Roch to Smithy Bridge. Historic England lists the building as Grade II* (List Entry Number 1309615), dated to about 1610 and probably built for Theophilus Ashton; the list entry gives the grid reference SD9224214490 and a full architectural description of the porch, mullioned windows and interior features. These are matters of record you can look up on the National Heritage List for England. (Historic England's entry is the clearest, contemporary source for the building itself.)

The boggart story that brings visitors and late walkers to peer at the windows is older in print than the present stone house. Nineteenth century folklorists recorded a dramatic tradition: a grasping uncle, two orphan children disposed of so that the estate could be seized, and the afterwards-haunting of the place by a “Clegg Hall Boggart.” John Roby published a version in his Traditions of Lancashire; local writers and collectors repeated variants and an associated ballad. These accounts are the primary sources for the tale as a piece of Lancashire folk narrative.

Local historians have been explicit about the difference between the two kinds of source. The 1889 History of the Parish of Rochdale (Butterworth) notes the same tradition but warns that Roby’s retelling is “pure imagination” and that, although a ghost tradition was current in living memory and even gave rise to the local proverb “As ill as Clegg Hall boggart,” the violent episode is not supported by contemporary legal or manorial records cited in the book. In short, the building and its succession of owners are documented; the murderous episode lives in oral tradition and Victorian collectors' pages.

What the archives do show is a traceable ownership and building history. Butterworth’s parish history and the Victoria County History note the medieval family names associated with the site, the sale of the “capital messuage of Clegg called Clegg Hall” in the early 17th century, and the present house’s likely early-17th-century date. Historic England cites those county histories in its list entry for the architectural description. Those documentary strands are evidence of place and people; they do not, however, supply a contemporaneous 13th- or 14th-century record proving the murders described in the boggart legend.

That distinction matters because Victorian and earlier collectors often shaped and embellished what they heard. Folklore collectors were not court clerks; they recorded stories people told, sometimes smoothing gaps with imaginative detail. The Clegg Hall boggart is one of several regional boggarts recorded in Lancashire folklore, a useful example of how local names and proverbs can preserve a tale even when the archival trail is thin.

So does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall? If you mean “is there an archival, contemporaneous record that the alleged murders took place and left restless spirits?” the answer is no: researchers citing the local histories and the National Heritage List find no surviving medieval court roll or inquest that corroborates the dramatic crime as a documented fact. If you mean “is the boggart alive as a story?” the answer is yes: the spirit survives in printed folklore, in local sayings and in the imagination of visitors and readers.

If you want to follow the trail yourself, two good starting points are the Historic England listing for the house (for verified architectural and legal status) and the nineteenth century sources that collected the tale, notably John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and Butterworth’s History of the Parish of Rochdale, which explicitly separates the tradition from the documentary record. Those sources show where the story comes from and where the solid evidence begins and ends; beyond that the rest belongs to local legend and its afterlife in print and conversation.

articles.title: Upcoming services and events at st Luke’s Church, Deeplish
articles.excerpt: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish is hosting several community events this week, including a Holy Communion service and a women’s breakfast.
articles.content_html:
St Luke’s Church in Deeplish is set to hold a service of Holy Communion on October 25 at 10am, officiated by Revd Sylvia Barron. Following the service, attendees are invited to enjoy tea or coffee and engage in conversation, fostering a sense of community among participants.

Additionally, on October 28, the church will host a Bible study group at 10am, welcoming anyone interested in exploring the Bible in a friendly and informal setting. Later that day, at 11am, there will be a Morning Praise service led by Reader Sue Horobin, open to both regular members and newcomers.

This morning, the church is also hosting a women’s breakfast from 9am to 10:30am in the parish room. This event offers a chance for women to connect with friends and meet new people, with breakfast provided free of charge.

The main service on October 29 will begin at 10:30am, focusing on Matthew, chapter nine, verses 18 to 24. The church encourages anyone who hasn’t attended before to come as they are, with refreshments available after the service.

articles.title: The Healey Dell prophecy: Eleanor Byron, Mother Bagden and what the records actually show
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
articles.summary: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge — the Thrutch — is one of Rochdale borough’s most durable story‑places. The best‑known version of the tale says a local noblewoman, usually called Lady Eleanor (later linked by tellings to the Byron family), visited a fortune‑teller named Mother Bagden; the woman predicted Eleanor would be a maid, a wife and a widow all in one day, and on her wedding night the bridegroom was killed. That dramatic sequence appears in the earliest printed collections of Lancashire lore and in the Dell’s modern visitor material, but the story’s status changes sharply once you separate nineteenth‑century collectors from contemporary medieval records. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

The oldest printed witness we can point to is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire, a book of collected oral tales published in the early 1800s; Roby preserves a long, romance‑style narrative set at Healey that includes a miller, a ‘Fairies’ Chapel’, a talisman and the fatal wedding night that fulfils the prophecy. Roby’s purpose was to record local storytelling rather than to provide documentary proof of medieval events, and his account reads as literary folklore rather than archival history. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Local antiquarians and guidebooks of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries amplified Roby’s version. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s trail guides and a short history leaflet reproduce the same outline: Ralph the miller, a messenger, Mother Bagden who claims intimate contact with a Fairy Queen, and the prediction that Eleanor will be “maid, wife and widow” in one day, followed by the death of her groom in a family feud. Those local guides attribute their narrative to older local histories such as William Robertson’s writings. The Heritage Centre presents the material as local myth and interpretation, alongside explanations of the Dell’s geology and industrial archaeology. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

What is demonstrably factual? Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve and visitor attraction at 121 Dell Road, with industrial archaeology (old mill sites, lodges) and a prominent Victorian railway viaduct that now forms part of a riverside trail. The viaduct is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those physical and administrative facts are public and documentable. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

What is folklore and what is missing from the archive? The supernatural elements — a Fairy Queen with prophetic power, spells that cause a bridegroom’s death, a named medieval Lady Eleanor whose wedding‑night fate is attested in contemporary court rolls or parish registers — lack contemporary documentary support. The story’s appearance in sources begins with nineteenth‑century collectors (Roby) and later local antiquarians (for example William Robertson as cited in modern guides); no contemporaneous medieval legal documents or parish entries confirming the prophecy or the precise characters named in the tale have been produced in those printed sources. In short: the prophecy belongs to the region’s oral and printed folklore tradition rather than to verified medieval record. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Why the story endures is straightforward: Healey Dell’s dramatic rock cleft, the Thrutch, looks for stories. A recess by the river invites the idea of a “Fairies’ Chapel”, and the valley’s history of mills, local rival families and visible ruins supplied the narrative scaffolding that collectors and guidebook writers later filled with characters and prophecy. The Heritage Centre explicitly treats the tale as part of the Dell’s storytelling — useful to visitors but not presented as archival fact. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

If you want to follow the trace yourself: read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed narrative; consult the Healey Dell Heritage Centre material for the local retelling and references to later antiquarians; and visit the Dell to see the viaduct, the Thrutch and the mill remains that inspired the story. If you hope to find a medieval legal record proving the prophecy, those proving documents are not cited in the early printed collectors and have not been produced in the local guides that preserve the tale — which is why historians and the Heritage Centre treat it as legend, however rooted in local memory it may be. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The tale of Lady Eleanor, Mother Bagden and the Fairies’ Chapel at Healey Dell is well attested in local printed collectors — but it survives as folklore, not as a documented medieval event.
articles.summary: The tale of Lady Eleanor, Mother Bagden and the Fairies’ Chapel at Healey Dell is well attested in local printed collectors — but it survives as folklore, not as a documented medieval event.
articles.body:
Ask a local where the Fairies’ Chapel is and they’ll point you down the steps from Station Road, into the ravine by the River Spodden. Ask whether fairies live there and the practical answer is simple: no verifiable evidence supports the existence of fairies; what the records do show is a named rock formation, a cluster of old stories collected in the nineteenth century and a long history of people visiting the site because the place feels, to many, a little uncanny. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

Those are not trivial facts. Healey Dell is a designated Local Nature Reserve and an area of industrial archaeology that straddles borough boundaries; part of the valley was legally made a statutory LNR in April 1976. The most dramatic built feature is the Healey Dell Viaduct, a high, eight‑arched sandstone railway viaduct that is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those designations are documentary and can be checked. ([rossendale.gov.uk](https://www.rossendale.gov.uk/download/meetings/id/4148/e2_appendix_2))

The Dell’s historical record is everyday, material and useful. The valley contains the remains of nineteenth‑century mills and the disused Rochdale‑to‑Bacup railway line; archaeological and conservation surveys catalogue those features and guide how the reserve is managed for wildlife and visitors. Management is led locally by Rochdale (and neighbouring Rossendale) authorities and by volunteer groups; published ecological reports and neighbourhood plans reference Healey Dell when mapping green infrastructure for the area. That is the part of the story that affects readers’ lives—path repairs, parking signage, listed‑building consent for the viaduct—because those are things the council, landowners and statutory consultees can change. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

The Fairies’ Chapel and the Healey Dwarf belong to a different archive: folklore. Nineteenth‑century writers and local collectors, notably the county antiquarian tradition and later local compilers, set down tales about a natural recess in the rock that looked a little like an altar and could be called a chapel. Early print references—quoted in modern guides—describe a hidden pulpit‑like formation revealed when a flood washed away a covering ledge; later colourful retellings add a Fairy Queen, a Fairy King and a bewitched dwarf or witch‑figure, motifs common to British fairy lore. Those stories come from literary and folkloric sources rather than parish registers, court records or archaeological excavation reports; they are valuable for what they tell us about local imagination and nineteenth‑century reading habits, not as evidence of the supernatural. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

You can still see the place‑name on the ground. Local walking leaflets and heritage trails mark a route down to the feature and signposts to a ‘Fairy Chapel’ appear on nearby footpaths and at the steps off Station Road. Community events and the Tearooms’ heritage material reproduce the old legends for visitors, which keeps the stories alive. None of these modern references change the distinction: a name, an attractive rock formation and repeated storytelling are not proof of otherworldly residents. ([whitworth.gov.uk](https://www.whitworth.gov.uk/uploads/walkingdocuments/files/WALK%206%20Healey%20Dell%20-%20captioned%20viaduct.pdf))

What remains uncertain—and worth noting—is provenance. Some of the best‑known versions of the Healey tales were shaped by nineteenth‑century collectors and local storytellers; when folklore circulates in print, oral tradition and tourism literature it can harden into ‘local history’ in popular memory. Where claims involve specific historical persons, dates or events, they should be tested against archival material; in the case of the Fairies’ Chapel, the archive records the place and the stories about it, not supernatural events. If you want proof, visit the council‑maintained reserve, look up the Historic England listing for the viaduct and read the nineteenth‑century sources for yourself—then decide whether the place’s atmosphere does the rest. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))
articles.content_html:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge, the Thrutch, has long been a place that invites stories. Visitors still stand under the Victorian viaduct, follow the path to the small pool visitors call the Fairies’ Chapel, and hear the familiar local version: a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden prophesied that a noblewoman, usually named Lady Eleanor (later linked with the Byron family), would be a maiden, a wife and a widow in one day; on her wedding day the bridegroom was slain and the prophecy fulfilled.

That dramatic sequence is not a modern invention. The earliest printed form widely available to readers comes from the 19th century: John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire preserves a long, romance‑style account set at Healey that gives the tale its shape and characters. Later local antiquarians — notably William Robertson in his regional histories — recycled and amplified the narrative, and modern site interpretation at Healey Dell Heritage Centre follows that printed tradition when it tells visitors the Fairies’ Chapel story.

What is verifiable fact? Healey Dell is a named Local Nature Reserve and visitor attraction at Dell Road, with recognisable industrial archaeology (mill sites, lodges) and a prominent Grade II listed viaduct built for the Lancashire and Yorkshire extension railway in 1869–70. Those are public, documentable features you can still see. The Heritage Centre publishes its own guides that describe the gorge, the so‑called Fairies’ Chapel and the local legends; Rochdale Borough Council lists the reserve, its address, opening details and facilities. The viaduct is recorded on the National Heritage List for England. These are the things you can check on official records and by visiting.

What is folklore? The supernatural elements — a Fairy Queen who issues prophecies, a witch‑fortune‑teller who communes with her, or the idea that a named medieval Lady Eleanor’s fate is attested in contemporary legal or parish records — belong to oral tradition and antiquarian storytelling. Roby, Robertson and later guide‑book writers recorded what people were telling in their own times rather than producing medieval documents. Local interpretation today openly presents the story as legend rather than as archival history.

How the story changed over time is itself revealing. Roby’s early 19th‑century text gives a literary, sometimes florid narrative with named characters: a miller, a talisman, Oliver Chadwyke and a Lady Eleanor. Later retellings folded in local family names (Byron, Chadwick) and local topography (the Thrutch, the Fairies’ Chapel). The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s material adapts those versions when it points visitors to the rock formation and to the flood of 1838 that altered the gorge and submerged some of the features said to be the ‘chapel’. That lineage — oral tale into printed folklore into heritage interpretation — is a common path for many English place legends.

What cannot be shown from surviving records is the medieval documentary backbone the story implies. I found no contemporary 15th‑century court rolls, parish registers or legal documents that confirm a wedding‑night killing, a named Lady Eleanor Byron of the period, or a recorded prophetic witch in Healey Dell. Where claims cannot be matched to contemporary archives, the careful historian treats them as tradition and story. The result is not dismissal but classification: good material for local imagination, caution for anyone treating it as proven history.

If you want to see the story’s sources for yourself: read John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed tale, inspect the Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s guide for the way the tale is now presented on site, and consult Rochdale Borough Council and the National Heritage List for England for the reserve’s practical and architectural facts. The prophecy endures because place, geology and a few dramatic printed versions make for memorable storytelling. That is a valuable local inheritance — so long as readers keep legend and archive in separate pockets.

Practical details: Healey Dell Nature Reserve and the Heritage Centre are listed by Rochdale Borough Council (address Dell Road, Healey). The viaduct is Grade II listed on Historic England’s National Heritage List. For maps, opening times and the Heritage Centre’s explanatory leaflets, use the council and the centre’s published material.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council invites feedback on proposed Customer Access strategy
articles.excerpt: Residents are encouraged to share their views on the proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy, which aims to enhance how the public interacts with the Council over the next five years.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has launched a consultation inviting residents to provide feedback on its proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy for the next five years. The strategy aims to simplify how residents contact the Council and ensure they receive consistent support, whether online, by phone, or in person.

The Council has identified six priorities for enhancing customer access and nine pledges detailing what residents can expect from the service. The aim is to create a seamless experience for users, allowing them to receive assistance without needing to navigate the Council's organisational structure. The Council emphasises the importance of making it easy for individuals to access the right help, especially during challenging times.

Residents can review the draft strategy and related documents, including the Equality Impact Assessment and Sustainability Impact Assessment, on the Council's consultation hub. The Council is keen to know if the proposed priorities resonate with the community and whether any aspects have been overlooked. The consultation documents are available for review and can be accessed through the Council's website.

The consultation is open now, and residents are encouraged to participate to help shape the final version of the strategy. Feedback can be submitted through the Council's website until the consultation period closes. This initiative represents an opportunity for the community to influence how the Council interacts with its residents over the coming years.

articles.title: Plans submitted for demolition of seven blocks on Lower Falinge Estate in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing has submitted plans to demolish seven blocks on the Lower Falinge Estate to make way for 270 new homes, aiming to improve living conditions in the area.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has submitted plans to Rochdale Council for the demolition of seven blocks on the Lower Falinge Estate, with the aim of constructing 270 new homes. The blocks earmarked for demolition include Ollerton, Newstead, Romsey, Quinton, Ullesthorpe, Zedburgh, and Vaynor, which have been identified as no longer providing safe and warm living conditions.

The proposed redevelopment will primarily take place on land adjacent to Sheriff Street and Falinge Road, with additional plots near Redcross Street also included in the plans. RBH has indicated that the new homes will be a mix of houses and flats, all available for social rent, and designed to meet modern energy efficiency standards.

The plans come after a previous attempt to demolish the blocks was halted by a legal challenge from residents, who argued that there was no clear regeneration plan following the demolition. However, RBH has now provided a detailed regeneration strategy, which includes creating new landscaping, public open spaces, and safer streets, as well as improved walking routes into Rochdale town centre.

One resident, Andy Roche, who currently occupies Zedburgh, expressed distress over the plans, stating that he feels the needs of residents have not been adequately considered. Despite being offered alternative housing options, he claims none meet his current living standards. RBH has stated that they have engaged with local residents and stakeholders to ensure the new homes reflect community priorities.

articles.title: Jolly Josh Christmas Ball sells out as Rochdale businesses urged to help
articles.excerpt: The Castleton charity is asking businesses to sponsor a table for £50 or donate raffle and auction prizes ahead of its December ball at Rochdale Town Hall.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh has filled the guest tables for its Jolly Jingle Christmas Ball and is now asking local businesses to help turn a full room into vital funding for families.

The ball takes place at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 11 December at 7pm. With guest places filled, the charity is inviting businesses across Rochdale and Greater Manchester to sponsor tables for £50, donate raffle or auction prizes, or discuss other ways to support the evening.

A contribution does not have to be extravagant. Vouchers, meals, products, experiences and services can all help boost the fundraising total.

Based at Ensor Mill on Queensway in Castleton, Jolly Josh says it supports more than 300 families of children and young people with complex medical needs, physical disabilities, life limiting conditions, and profound and multiple learning disabilities.

Its purpose built centre offers hydrotherapy, rebound therapy, sensory activities, youth social groups, accessible after school provision and support for parents and carers.

The charity says it receives no regular government funding, making grants, donations, community fundraising and business support essential to keeping its services running.

Rose Hutchings, Lead Fundraiser at Jolly Josh, said:

“We’ve been absolutely delighted by the response to this year’s Jolly Jingle Ball and to see the tables fill. What we’d really love now is for the wider Rochdale business community to help us make the night as successful as possible for our families.

“A £50 table sponsorship or a donated raffle or auction prize might feel like a relatively small contribution to a business, but when lots of local organisations get behind us those contributions quickly add up.

“Jolly Josh doesn’t receive regular government funding, so fundraising and community support genuinely help us continue providing a safe, accessible place where children and young people with complex needs and their families can connect, access opportunities and feel part of a community.”

The appeal comes as demand for the charity’s specialist services continues to grow. Jolly Josh says its hydrotherapy provision has previously run at least 42 sessions a week and experienced waiting lists, with strong demand for other services too.

Businesses interested in a £50 table sponsorship, donating a raffle or auction prize, or offering other event support can email Rose Hutchings at rose@jollyjosh.co.uk or call 01706 399141.

Further information about Jolly Josh, registered charity number 1178116, is available at https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

articles.title: Rochdale’s £5m crisis support fund: what help is available this winter and how to ask
articles.excerpt: The council lists help with sudden financial emergencies, housing costs and essential goods. Different schemes have different rules; an award is not automatic.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale residents struggling to afford essentials can ask about support through the council's Crisis and Resilience Fund as winter approaches.

The £5 million programme runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, using Department for Work and Pensions funding. It replaced the Household Support Fund in April. The £5 million is the borough-wide programme budget, not an amount available to each household.

The council lists several routes: Crisis Payments for sudden financial difficulty; Housing Payments for emergency rent or housing costs; the Discretionary Crisis Fund for goods; and Healthy Homes grants for eligible vulnerable residents needing help such as boiler repairs or essential appliances. Each route needs its own eligibility check.

For Crisis Payments, eligible residents can receive a voucher worth up to £75 towards food and energy. Applicants must live in Rochdale borough, be at least 16 and have nobody receiving Child Benefit for them. Applications are allowed once every six months. Apply by calling 01706 923685; the published hours are Monday to Friday, 9am–5pm. Examples of a crisis include fire, flooding, a health emergency or losing employment.

The separate Discretionary Crisis Fund is described as last-resort support. It provides goods rather than cash. Its contact number is 01706 532222 and its email is StrategicHousing@rochdale.gov.uk.

Check the route that matches your circumstances before applying. The main fund page also mentions food vouchers only through the end of the 2026 summer holidays; that wording does not establish a winter voucher entitlement.

articles.title: Harvest Thanksgiving service to be held in Rochdale on October 17

A Harvest Thanksgiving service is scheduled for Sunday, October 17, at 10.30am in Rochdale. The event aims to celebrate the abundance of creation and raise awareness of the need to support those less fortunate in the community.

Led by Rev’d Ben Somervell, the service will include a sermon based on Psalm 126. Attendees are encouraged to bring donations of tinned and dry packaged foods for the local foodbank, highlighting the importance of community support during challenging times.

The service is designed for all ages and will feature performances from the day school choir, who will sing a selection of songs. Following the service, refreshments including coffee and tea will be served in the parish room, providing an opportunity for fellowship and conversation.

Everyone is welcome to attend, regardless of their previous church experience or beliefs. The evening will also include a relaxed prayer meeting, offering a space for reflection and preparation for the week ahead.

articles.title: Broadfield Park Slopes renovation celebrated at Rochdale Town Hall
articles.excerpt: A special event at Rochdale Town Hall recognised the contributions of volunteers and partners involved in the restoration of Broadfield Park Slopes, highlighting the project's community impact and heritage significance.
articles.content_html:
A celebration was held at Rochdale Town Hall to honour the individuals and groups who contributed to the renovation of Broadfield Park Slopes. This historic site, located between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church, has undergone significant restoration, thanks to the efforts of local volunteers and funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The event, organised by Polly Brant, Cultural Engagement Officer for Rochdale Council, brought together volunteers, partners, and community members to acknowledge their roles in the project. Guests were treated to a series of films by local filmmaker Jack Grindrod, showcasing the stories and heritage associated with the park's transformation. The films captured the community involvement that played a crucial role in the renovation process.

The evening featured poetry readings by Alende Amisi, a local poet and former young poet in residence, who shared his personal reflections on Rochdale's heritage. His contributions added a personal touch to the event, which celebrated not only the park's restoration but also the community spirit that drove the project forward.

The renovation has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, and introduced new heritage interpretation. The lower lawn has been terraced to create a natural amphitheatre, providing a new space for activities and events, enhancing the park's role as a community hub.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Town celebrates the people and stories behind Broadfield Park Slopes renovation - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Town celebrates the people and stories behind Broadfield Park Slopes renovation The people who helped bring Rochdale’s historic Broadfield Park Slopes back to life were celebrated at a special event at Rochdale Town Hall. The celebration, arranged by Polly Brant, Rochdale Council Cultural Engagement officer, brought together volunteers, partners and people who have been involved in the project to recognise what has been achieved and, importantly, the contribution local people have made along the way. Guests watched a series of films created by Rochdale filmmaker Jack Grindrod and Breaking Barriers, capturing the people, stories, heritage and community involvement behind the transformation. The evening also featured poetry readings from Alende Amisi, a poet who grew up in Rochdale and was a young poet in residence during Rochdale’s Town of Culture. Passionate about the town and its heritage, Alende brought a personal perspective to an evening which was as much about Rochdale’s people as its history. A special thank you was also given to the many volunteers who have supported the project, giving their time to archaeological digs, activities and events and helping uncover and share the history of this important part of the town. The Grade II listed Broadfield Park Slopes sit between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church and have been restored through a project delivered by Rochdale Development Agency working with Rochdale Borough Council, with funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund. The work has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, lighting and CCTV, and introduced new heritage interpretation. The lower lawn has also been terraced, creating a natural amphitheatre and new space for activities and events. READ MORE: Customers flock to opening of new Peacocks store Archaeology and community participation have been a major part of the project. Excavations have uncovered the footings of Charles Kershaw’s 19th century Central Corn Mill, cobbled trackways and the former public weigh station, alongside finds including ceramics, clay smoking pipes, animal bones and glass bottles. Four archaeological digs have taken place, with the wider programme involving schoolchildren, students, volunteers and members of the public. It has included 28 work placement students, 12 archaeological volunteers and a two year schools programme involving 715 pupils. Cllr Sue Smith, portfolio holder for Communities and Co-operation at Rochdale Council, said: “This was a wonderful opportunity to celebrate not just the transformation of the Broadfield Park Slopes, but the people who have made this project so special. “Our volunteers deserve a huge thank you. They have given their time, enthusiasm and energy to this project and have helped us uncover and share more of Rochdale’s history. “It was fantastic to see those stories captured in the films created by Jack Grindrod and Breaking Barriers, and to hear from Alende Amisi, whose passion for Rochdale and its heritage really reflects what this project is about. “The Slopes have been part of Rochdale for generations. We have protected an important part of our heritage, opened it back up for people to enjoy and, crucially, involved our communities in doing it.” The Broadfield Park Slopes are now open to the public, creating a restored green space at the heart of Rochdale’s historic town centre. articles.title: Young people inspire £85,000–£100,000 Castleton pump track proposal
articles.excerpt: A site beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road is being explored for a Castleton bike track, with young people helping shape the idea. Funding and approvals remain outstanding.
articles.content_html:
A new pump track costing an estimated £85,000 to £100,000 is being explored for Castleton after local young people asked for somewhere closer to home to ride their bikes.

Councillor Dave Jones said an area beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road had emerged as a promising potential location following discussions with council officers and youth workers.

The proposal remains at an early stage. No funding or final site approval has been announced, and there is no confirmed construction timetable.

In an update shared with Rochdale Daily, Cllr Jones described a positive meeting with Environmental Management, township officer Caroline and Jasmin from the Youth Work Team to discuss the concept.

Several possible locations were considered. According to the councillor, young people suggested the Manchester Road site because it feels safe. Its existing play area and car park could also make it convenient for families with children of different ages.

The idea is for younger children to use the playground while older children and teenagers could enjoy a nearby bike track, bringing different activities together in one central location.

Cllr Jones said those at the meeting supported involving young people in the design process. They also discussed whether contractors could explain how the track is built and explore suitable opportunities for young people to participate.

A bike repair hub was another suggestion. Local young people have spoken about their interest in repairing bicycles and sharing those skills with others. Secure bike storage lockers were also raised during the discussions.

The councillor said some young people currently travel to tracks elsewhere in the borough, including Littleborough, and expressed concern about the busy roads those journeys can involve. He believes a Castleton facility could offer a more convenient option and reassurance for families.

Funding is the main obstacle. Cllr Jones put the initial estimated cost at between £85,000 and £100,000 and said several processes and approvals would need to be completed before any scheme could proceed.

Council officers are now exploring possible funding sources, according to his update. A further meeting is planned to discuss potential designs and ensure any future proposal reflects what local young people want.

Cllr Jones also thanked Keane, the young person who first approached him with the idea, and praised young residents for taking an active role in improving their community.

He cautioned: “It's important to stress that projects like this take time, and there is still a long way to go.”

The potential location, repair hub, storage lockers and construction involvement are all ideas under discussion rather than confirmed features of an approved scheme.

Would your family use a pump track in Castleton, and what would you like a future design to include? Share your views in the comments.

articles.title: Rochdale Council celebrates achievements of over 200 cared-for children at annual awards
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council hosted its annual awards ceremony at Matthew Moss High School, recognising the achievements of more than 200 cared-for children with medals and a day of entertainment.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council held its annual awards ceremony on 16 October at Matthew Moss High School, celebrating the achievements of over 200 cared-for children. The event, known as 'Our Big Day', recognised the resilience and determination of young people in care, with hundreds of medals awarded to honour their individual successes.

The council received 273 nominations from carers, teachers, and social workers, highlighting the inspiring journeys of children up to the age of 12. Awards were given for exceptional progress in education, sporting achievements, acts of kindness, and positive attitudes in the face of adversity. The day included a variety of entertainment, such as trampolines, funfair rides, and face painting, allowing families to create joyful memories together.

Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, expressed her pride in the achievements of the children, stating, "They are all exceptional young people and show phenomenal determination to be their very best. This doesn’t go unnoticed by those around them." The event aimed to provide public recognition for the hard work and accomplishments of these young individuals.

Local businesses sponsored the celebration, contributing to the activities and entertainment provided for families. Notable sponsors included A&T Surfacing Ltd, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, and Rochdale Hornets, among others. This community support helped create a memorable day for the children and their families.

articles.title: Jolly Josh welcomes Rochdale families with inclusive play, music and activity sessions
articles.excerpt: The Castleton charity is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with weekly sessions and bookable activities.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with a programme of inclusive activities and support.

Based at 2 Ensor Mill in Castleton, Rochdale, OL11 2NU, the centre welcomes children and young adults aged from birth to 19.

The charity says finding activities where a child is welcomed, understood and supported can be difficult, and wants more parents, carers, relatives and professionals to know what is available.

Its programme includes music and signing, themed play sessions, an after-school club, a youth group and activities that families can book directly with the centre.

Weekly sessions

Sing And Sign runs every Wednesday from 10.30am to 12.30pm, bringing together music, songs and signing to make communication fun.

Themed Stay And Play takes place every Tuesday and Saturday from 9.30am to 12.30pm. Sessions offer activities, friendship and a different theme each week.

Sensory Touch And Music runs every Thursday from 10am to noon, offering a relaxing sensory session.

The After School Club takes place every Wednesday from 4pm to 7pm, with inclusive activities and a light tea offered for every child.

The Youth Group meets every Thursday from 5pm to 8pm, giving young people a welcoming space to socialise, take part in activities and build friendships.

Activities available to book

Hydrotherapy sessions can be booked for families or with the centre’s Hydro Lead.

Private sound bath sessions are also available by contacting the centre, offering an opportunity to take time out of a busy schedule.

Rebound Therapy provides supported movement and sensory experiences using a trampoline, with sessions bookable through the centre.

How to get in touch

Parents, carers, family members and professionals supporting a child with complex medical needs are invited to contact Jolly Josh to learn more about its sessions.

Call 01706 399141, email sarah@jollyjosh.co.uk or visit https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

The centre asks anyone planning to visit to contact the team first so an appointment can be arranged.

Families can contact the centre to discuss which sessions suit their child and ask about booking, availability and charges.

The charity is also encouraging people to share its appeal with families who may not yet know about the support available.

articles.title: Volunteers urgently needed at Hollingworth Lake to help Rochdale Sea Cadets
articles.excerpt: GTAS is appealing for volunteers and a donated skip to help clear an overgrown storage area for Rochdale Sea Cadets on Saturday 24 October, meeting at 10am.
articles.content_html:
GTAS has issued an urgent appeal for volunteers to help clear an overgrown storage area for Rochdale Sea Cadets this Saturday, 24 October.

Anyone able to lend a hand is asked to meet at Hollingworth Lake council car park at 10am. Organisers say help would be welcome for any length of time, whether volunteers can spare an hour or stay for the day.

The group describes the clearance as a big task and is asking people to bring sturdy gardening gloves if they have them. Spades, shovels, loppers, other gardening tools and wheelbarrows would also be useful.

Local businesses are being asked to support the effort too. GTAS is looking for a skip or waste company willing to donate a skip for a few hours to help with the clearance.

The volunteer day is an opportunity for residents and businesses to give practical support to Rochdale Sea Cadets by helping bring the overgrown space back into use.

Anyone who can volunteer or help provide a skip should message GTAS directly through the group’s appeal post.

Could you spare an hour on Saturday, or do you know a business that could help? Share the appeal and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

Source: GTAS community appeal supplied to Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Volunteers and council team tackle overgrown areas at Middleton’s Jubilee Park
articles.excerpt: The Friends of Jubilee Park and council staff have joined forces for the second phase of work to manage overgrown shrubs and care for the park’s rhododendrons.
articles.content_html:
Work to open up overgrown shrub areas at Jubilee Park in Middleton has entered its second phase, with volunteers and council staff joining forces to improve the grounds.

The Friends of Jubilee Park have been working alongside Rochdale Borough Council’s Environmental Management team, carrying out maintenance that includes caring for the park’s collection of rhododendrons.

The group says the work will encourage healthy new growth over the next couple of seasons, improve views and sight lines, and help visitors feel safer.

Opening up densely planted areas is intended to create a brighter, more welcoming park while supporting the long-term health of its shrubs.

Visitors may notice that some sections look temporarily untidy as the work progresses. The Friends have asked for patience, explaining that the maintenance is intended to bring lasting improvements.

“These improvements will bring lasting benefits for visitors and help Jubilee Park continue to thrive,” the group said.

The Friends describe Jubilee Park as a Gold Medal-winning Green Flag park and thanked visitors for their understanding while volunteers and staff care for the grounds.

The latest work forms part of an ongoing effort to maintain the much-loved Middleton green space for everyone who uses it.

Source: Friends of Jubilee Park update supplied to Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Inclusive roundabout and zip line feature in plans for new Falinge Park play area
articles.excerpt: Mayoress Iram Faisal has unveiled plans for new play equipment at Falinge Park, including a wheelchair-accessible roundabout, an inclusive seesaw and a double cableway zip line.
articles.content_html:
Plans for a new play area at Falinge Park have been unveiled, with wheelchair-accessible equipment among the attractions proposed for children and families.

Mayoress Iram Faisal shared details of the project, describing it as a deeply personal undertaking in the park where she played as a child.

The proposed equipment includes a double cableway zip line with ramps; a toddler multi-play unit; toddler and junior swings; an inclusive seesaw; a Crazy Gander springer; and a wheelchair-accessible roundabout.

In her announcement, Mrs Faisal said inclusivity had been central to the vision, with the aim of helping more children enjoy the park together.

“Every child deserves the opportunity to play, explore and enjoy their childhood,” she said.

For the Mayoress, the plans also carry memories of her own upbringing.

“Having lived here and played in this very park myself, to now be in a position to play a part in transforming it for the next generation has been an incredibly emotional journey,” she said.

She thanked councillors Faisal Rana and Amber Nisa, Rochdale Borough Council and its Environmental Management Team, alongside everyone involved in bringing the project forward.

Mrs Faisal said the improvements were about investing in children and creating a space where families could make memories together.

“From playing in Falinge Park as a child to helping shape its future, this really is a full-circle moment,” she added.

The announcement refers to a hoped-for start towards the end of February, with work continuing into March, subject to final arrangements. It does not specify the year or confirm an opening date, so that timetable remains to be clarified.

Residents have been invited to share their views on the proposals.

Source: announcement by Mayoress Iram Faisal, supplied to Rochdale Daily and published on her public Facebook page: https://www.facebook.com/iram.faisal.5095/posts/1764829918060894/

articles.title: Rochdale social worker Nneamaka Uti shortlisted for national award
articles.excerpt: Nneamaka Uti, who works in Rochdale Council’s adult care service, is a finalist in the Social Worker of the Year Awards, with winners announced on 22 October.
articles.content_html:
A social worker helping adults in Rochdale has been shortlisted for a national award recognising outstanding work in the profession.

Nneamaka Uti, who works in Rochdale Borough Council’s adult care service, is a finalist for Newly Qualified Adult Social Worker of the Year at the 2026 Social Worker of the Year Awards.

The winners will be announced on Thursday 22 October, at an awards reception in London. The organisers have confirmed that the afternoon event will run from 2pm to 5pm.

Councillor Shah Wazir, the council’s cabinet member for adult care, welcomed the recognition.

He said: “This is lovely and deserved recognition for Nneamaka and showcases Rochdale’s caring side at its very best. Following adult care’s good CQC rating this underlines the high-quality care and support the council is delivering for residents across the borough. Best of luck to Nneamaka at the awards ceremony.”

The council’s announcement links Nneamaka’s shortlisting with the adult care service’s good Care Quality Commission rating, highlighting the contribution of staff supporting residents across the borough.

Now marking their 20th anniversary, the Social Worker of the Year Awards recognise achievements across children’s and adult social work in England. This year, the organisers have named 64 finalists across 14 categories.

Nneamaka is one of six finalists in the newly qualified adult social worker category. The shortlist recognises practitioners at the beginning of their careers, giving Rochdale a representative among those in contention for national recognition.

Gold and silver award recipients will be announced at the October reception.

Rochdale Daily wishes Nneamaka the best of luck.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Announces Free Bonfire Night Events for November 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will host three free firework displays across the borough in early November, featuring reduced noise fireworks for accessibility.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has confirmed a series of free firework displays to celebrate Bonfire Night in November 2026. The events will take place at three locations across the borough, including Middleton, Heywood, and Syke, with festivities beginning on Monday, November 2.

The first event will be held at Bowlee Community Park, located on Heywood Old Road in Middleton, starting at 6pm. The bonfire will be lit at 7pm, followed by fireworks at 7.30pm. The second display will occur on Tuesday, November 3, at Queen’s Park Road in Heywood, with the same timings. The final council-run event will take place on Wednesday, November 4, at Cronkeyshaw Common in Syke, also starting at 6pm.

In addition to the council events, Milnrow Cricket Club and Lobden Golf Club in Whitworth will host their own firework displays on Saturday, November 7. The Milnrow event will charge £7 for adults and £11.25 for families, while the Lobden Golf Club display will cost £5 for adults and £3 for children.

Rochdale Council has introduced reduced noise fireworks this year to make the displays more accessible for all attendees. The council advises visitors to walk or use public transport due to limited parking at the venues. Alcohol, fireworks, and sparklers are prohibited at all council-run events, and no toilet facilities will be available.

The council confirms the Rochdale display is on Wednesday 4 November 2026: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/481/rochdale-bonfire-and-fireworks-display

articles.title: Pacific, Mangos and Empire until morning: remembering Rochdale’s strip
articles.excerpt: Box-dye red hair, Jägerbombs and taxi queues that lasted hours—remembering Rochdale’s strip, its familiar faces and the venues keeping the town alive today.
articles.content_html:
Box-dye red hair, Jägerbombs and taxi queues that lasted hours—Rochdale’s nightlife in the 2000s and early 2010s was a whole chapter of growing up. And places such as Empire are still helping the town make memories.

There was a time when a night out in Rochdale came with its own wardrobe, soundtrack and familiar faces.

Box-dye red hair. Chinos. Ed Hardy. The infamous Rihanna jumper. Outfits that, looking back, were remarkably close to business casual—worn with complete confidence for a night on the strip.

Rihanna and Eminem provided the soundtrack. Ordering a Jägerbomb felt like an event. Pacific, Mangos, Litten Tree and Empire were names woven into the weekend.

Between the bars, the dancefloors and the eventual search for a taxi, Rochdale felt wonderfully alive.

One former glass collector and barmaid remembers an incredible scene: heaving venues, wonderful bouncers and, in her experience, few fights. When the night finally ended, queues for taxis could mean waiting for hours into the early morning.

The people who made the strip

Ask someone about their old nights out and they might start with a club. Before long, they will be talking about a person.

A favourite barmaid. A reassuring face on the door. Someone you always bumped into, whether you had arranged to meet or not.

Among those familiar faces was the man affectionately known to revellers as “the gas man”, remembered sitting at the corner of the strip.

The former bar worker recalls people stopping to hug him and give him money. Despite the difficult circumstances she remembers him facing, he was a beloved presence, recognised and greeted with affection.

His circumstances were his own, and a nickname cannot tell his whole story. But the warmth with which he is remembered belongs in the history of those nights, alongside the music and the venues.

The strip’s character came from its people.

From the glass collector’s side of the dancefloor

Working through those nights meant seeing what customers sometimes missed.

Collecting glasses through a crowded room. Keeping the bar moving. Watching the door team manage another wave of arrivals while friends tried to find one another inside.

The former worker remembers the bouncers warmly. Her account offers a different perspective from the assumption that a busy nightlife scene must have been defined by trouble: what stays with her is how enjoyable it was, how few fights she encountered and how much life filled the town centre.

That is a personal recollection, rather than a claim that every night passed without incident. But it captures something worth preserving—the pleasure of working somewhere everyone wanted to be.

What happened to Pacific, Mangos and Litten Tree?

Pacific, at 8 South Parade, is now listed as closed. An archived council entry records a premises-licence suspension beginning in July 2013 for non-payment of an annual fee or levy. That record does not, by itself, establish the venue’s final trading date or the full reasons it closed.

Sources: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/204/Detail?APP_ID=80078 and https://www.pubsgalore.co.uk/areas/rochdale-central/greater-manchester/

Mangos’ connection to a later venue remains visible in the paperwork. The council’s licensing record for Trinity retains conditions referring to the operating plan for Mango Bar at 3 King Street. The familiar address acquired another identity, although the sources reviewed do not establish the complete changeover story.

Source: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/203/Detail?LIC_ID=6700

Litten Tree’s premises at 10 Fleece Street subsequently became Yates and are now Courtyard Rochdale. CAMRA records its reopening under the Courtyard name in March 2024. For former regulars, the sign has changed, but the address remains somewhere people can meet for a night out.

Source: https://camra.org.uk/pubs/courtyard-rochdale-rochdale-153361

Empire: the night that kept going

Then there was Empire.

In the former bar worker’s memories, it was the infamous destination where the night could stretch towards 6am. Leaving meant discovering that the early morning had arrived while everyone was still enjoying themselves.

Empire remains part of Rochdale’s nightlife today. Its presently advertised Friday and Saturday hours run until 4am, with live bands and performances central to its programme.

Source: https://empirerochdale.co.uk/

Its contribution extends beyond an ordinary weekend. The council’s 2026 Feel Good Festival programme included performances throughout the day at Empire, followed by a midnight DJ slot.

Source: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/rochdale-feel-good-festival/indoor-venues

That continuing activity deserves recognition. Venues such as Empire give people a reason to come into Rochdale, meet friends, hear music and spend an evening in their own town.

The old strip cannot be recreated exactly. Its customers have grown older; their wardrobes, responsibilities and stamina may have changed.

But the affection remains—for the songs, the people, the staff who looked after everyone and the nights nobody wanted to finish.

Rochdale’s next great night out needs people willing to make it happen. Empire and the town’s other active venues are keeping that possibility alive.

What do you remember about the strip? Pacific or Mangos? Litten Tree before Empire? The Rihanna jumper, the Jägerbombs or the seemingly endless taxi queue? Share your memories—and give a mention to the bar staff, glass collectors and door teams who made those nights special.

articles.title: QTS Group hosts first safety Jamboree in Rochdale with over 350 attendees
articles.excerpt: The QTS Group's inaugural safety Jamboree at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale attracted more than 350 participants, focusing on health, safety, and innovation in the rail industry.
articles.content_html:
National rail contractor QTS Group hosted its first safety-focused Jamboree at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale, bringing together over 350 colleagues, supply chain partners, and activity hosts. The two-day event, which took place recently, was designed to promote health, safety, and innovation within the rail industry through interactive demonstrations and hands-on activities.

Attendees had the opportunity to engage with new technology and best practices from various suppliers and specialists. Jamie Marks, HSQE Manager at QTS Group, stated that the event aimed to foster knowledge sharing and strengthen relationships across the industry. He noted the positive feedback received and expressed enthusiasm for making next year's event even larger and more impactful.

Demonstrations included the Elios 3 drone for aerial mapping, virtual reality experiences simulating drone flights, and a confined space training simulator provided by Eurosafe. Participants also tested their skills on an excavator simulator from Flannery Plant Hire and witnessed mock aerial rescue demonstrations conducted by IRATA-trained teams.

The event not only highlighted the importance of safety in the rail sector but also provided a platform for networking and collaboration among industry professionals. QTS Group plans to build on this success for future events, aiming to further enhance safety practices in the rail industry.

articles.title: Hollingworth Lake to host Wave of Light walk remembering babies and children
articles.excerpt: Families affected by baby or child loss are invited to meet at Hollingworth Lake's beach at 6.30pm on Thursday 15 October for a remembrance walk and 7pm candle-lighting, with bereavement charities and helplines available for support.
articles.content_html:
Families and friends affected by the death of a baby or child are invited to gather at Hollingworth Lake in Littleborough on Thursday 15 October for a candlelit remembrance walk at the end of Baby Loss Awareness Week.

The community invitation asks people to meet at the beach at Hollingworth Lake at 6.30pm. The group plans to walk together around the lake, pausing approximately halfway round at a scenic point to light candles at 7pm as part of the worldwide Wave of Light.

The invitation is open to anyone who has experienced miscarriage, stillbirth, neonatal death, the death of a baby or the loss of a child at any age, as well as relatives, friends, neighbours and others wishing to show their support.

One of the people behind the gathering said that every year they light a candle for the babies they remember. This year, rather than marking the occasion alone, they hope people can come together for a shared moment of remembrance.

Baby Loss Awareness Week takes place each year from 9 to 15 October. At 7pm on 15 October, families around the world take part in the Wave of Light by lighting candles in memory of babies who have died. The Hollingworth Lake walk extends a welcome to those remembering children of all ages.

Those attending can bring a candle or battery-operated light, dress warmly for an October evening and carry a torch for the walk. Please keep a safe distance from the water, take care on paths after dark, never leave flames unattended, and take all candles and materials home rather than leaving them by or in the lake. Details of accessibility arrangements have not been provided in the original invitation.

EVENT DETAILS: Thursday 15 October 2026. Meet at 6.30pm at the beach at Hollingworth Lake, Littleborough, Rochdale, OL15 0AQ. Walk together and stop to light candles at 7pm. This article reports a community invitation; the charities listed below are support resources and are not described as organisers or sponsors of the event.

WHERE TO FIND HELP AFTER BABY OR CHILD LOSS

Grief can affect parents, partners, siblings, grandparents and friends, sometimes long after the death. No one has to attend the walk or speak about a loss to deserve support. The following verified organisations offer specialist information, listening services and, in some cases, counselling or local peer groups.

Sands — confidential help for anyone affected by pregnancy or baby loss, including bereaved relatives and friends. Free national helpline: 0808 164 3332; email: helpline@sands.org.uk; website: https://www.sands.org.uk/support-you/how-we-offer-support/helpline. Telephone hours are Monday to Friday 10am–3pm and Tuesday to Thursday 6pm–9pm, excluding bank holidays.

Child Bereavement UK — support for parents and carers when a baby or child dies, and for bereaved children and young people. Free helpline: 0800 02 888 40, Monday to Friday 8am–8pm, excluding bank holidays. Text or WhatsApp: 07418 341 800 (WhatsApp support for ages 13 and over). Website: https://www.childbereavementuk.org/.

Finding Rainbows — Greater Manchester peer support for families affected by early pregnancy loss or the death of a baby or child. Email: finding.rainbows@outlook.com; website: https://www.findingrainbows.org/.

Tommy's — specialist midwife-led advice on miscarriage, stillbirth, pregnancy after loss and pregnancy-related wellbeing. Free helpline: 0800 0147 800, Monday to Friday 9am–5pm. Email: midwife@tommys.org; website: https://www.tommys.org/. This is a non-urgent advice line.

The Lullaby Trust — specialist bereavement support after the sudden and unexpected death of a baby or young child. Free helpline: 0808 802 6868; website: https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/bereavement-support/find-support/. Phone support is available Monday to Friday 10am–2pm and weekends and public holidays 6pm–10pm.

Antenatal Results and Choices (ARC) — confidential, non-directive support after difficult antenatal test results, fetal diagnosis and pregnancy loss following a decision to end a pregnancy for medical reasons. Helpline: 020 7713 7486, Monday to Friday 10am–5.30pm. Text: 07908 683004; email: info@arc-uk.org; website: https://www.arc-uk.org/.

Miscarriage Association — information and support for anyone affected by miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or molar pregnancy. Website: https://www.miscarriageassociation.org.uk/.

Petals — specialist counselling for people affected by pregnancy loss, stillbirth or neonatal death, subject to service eligibility and referral arrangements. Website: https://www.petalscharity.org/.

4Louis — bereavement support resources and memory boxes for families following the death of a baby or child. Website: https://www.4louis.co.uk/.

SUDC UK — information, bereavement support and research relating to sudden unexplained death in childhood. Contact: 07880 350942, Monday to Thursday 9am–5pm; email: info@sudc.org.uk; website: https://sudc.org.uk/.

Greater Manchester NHS PETALS Perinatal Trauma and Loss Service — assessment and therapeutic support for people experiencing trauma related to birth, pregnancy or baby loss. A healthcare professional can make a referral. Telephone: 0161 271 0188 (option 4), Monday to Friday 9am–5pm; website: https://www.gmmh.nhs.uk/petals.

If you need somebody to talk to now, Samaritans offers free emotional support day and night on 116 123 (https://www.samaritans.org/). For urgent mental health support in England, contact NHS 111 and select the mental health option. Call 999 if someone is in immediate danger.

Whatever their age, and however much time has passed, every child deserves to be remembered. Those planning to attend are encouraged to offer one another kindness and space during the gathering.

articles.title: Rochdale Sleep Out raises almost £10,000 as organisers make final appeal
articles.excerpt: Supporters spent the night outdoors at the Crown Oil Arena for Petrus Community and Rochdale AFC Community Trust, with the annual charity Sleep Out now close to its £10,000 fundraising milestone.
articles.content_html:
Supporters from across Rochdale spent Friday night outdoors in solidarity with people experiencing homelessness, helping an annual charity Sleep Out raise almost £10,000.

The event, organised by Petrus Community and Rochdale AFC Community Trust, took place on Friday 9 October at the Crown Oil Arena. Participants were joined in the fundraising effort by donors and local businesses.

Petrus said the total was now approaching the £10,000 milestone and appealed for one final push to reach it. The figure is a provisional amount reported by the organisers, rather than a confirmed final total.

The Sleep Out aimed to raise awareness of housing insecurity and homelessness while giving participants a limited insight into the practical challenges of spending a night without a comfortable bed. Organisers stressed that taking part for one night cannot replicate the uncertainty and difficulties faced by people who have no safe place to call home.

Money raised will help sustain vital support for people experiencing homelessness and disadvantage. Petrus provides accommodation, housing advice, outreach, wellbeing support and opportunities to help people rebuild stability across Rochdale, Oldham and Burnley.

The partnership between Petrus and Rochdale AFC Community Trust also supports the Changing Lives programme, which uses football, wellbeing activities and pathways into education, volunteering and employment to help people experiencing homelessness or living in supported accommodation.

Last year's Sleep Out raised £7,875.52 for the two organisations. This year's organisers have thanked everyone who slept outdoors, donated or helped make the event possible.

Petrus is encouraging Rochdale residents who wish to support the final fundraising push to donate through its official website: https://www.petrus.org.uk/.

articles.title: Who
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure tied to Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel, showing what the oldest printed witnesses say and what is verifiable today.
articles.summary: A short guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure tied to Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel, showing what the oldest printed witnesses say and what is verifiable today.
articles.body:
Walkers who know Healey Dell will recognise the narrow cleft of the Spodden called the Thrutch and the little rock alcove that has long been known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel. The “Healey Dwarf” is the best‑known supernatural figure attached to that place: in local telling a tiny, ginger‑bearded person — sometimes imagined as a stone sentinel in the river — who belongs among the fairies. But the dwarf, like other elements of the Dell’s story‑map, belongs to folklore rather than to the archive of verifiable events.

The oldest printed witness for the tale that survives in wide circulation is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire. Roby collected and published local romances and legends in the early nineteenth century (his Lancashire volumes first appeared in 1829–31), and his chapter often cited as “The Fairies’ Chapel” gathers the characters and episodes — a cavern‑like cleft, a miller, a Fairy Queen and a small figure associated with the place — that later writers repeated and reshaped. Roby’s work is a primary source for the story as it was told in his era, but it must be read as a collector’s and storyteller’s account: it records oral tradition and contemporary retelling rather than offering documentary proof of supernatural events.

Later Victorian and local writers elaborated Roby’s material. A small book published in 1882, Healey Dell, or The History (in Verse) of Fairies: Meetings of the Fairy Queen and Healey Dwarf in the Fairy Chapel, gives a fully dramatised and poetical version in which a character called Healey (often pictured with a ginger beard in these retellings) is offered a place among the fairies and imagined as a stone guardian in the river. These later accounts are useful for tracking how the dwarf’s image — costume, beard and behaviour — became fixed in local imagination, but they are literary treatments rather than independent contemporary testimonies.

On the ground today the concrete facts are straightforward and separate from the stories. Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve with visible industrial archaeology — mill remains, waterfalls and the Victorian viaduct — and a heritage centre that presents the site’s history and folklore for visitors. The rock formation that inspired the name Fairies’ Chapel is a water‑worn niche; the site was altered by extreme flooding in the 1830s, and the physical features visible now are not identical to those seen by earlier visitors. Local authorities and the heritage centre present the dwarf and related tales as part of the Dell’s living folklore rather than as documented historical personages.

What we can say with confidence: the Healey Dwarf is a figure of local tradition preserved in nineteenth‑century printed collections and in later local retellings. The earliest reliable printed appearance is John Roby’s collection; later writers — including the 1882 verse volume — shaped the dwarf’s popular image. What cannot be verified from official records is any claim that a living dwarf or a supernatural guardian actually inhabited the Dell: there are no archival documents, legal records or contemporary official investigations that establish such a thing as historical fact.

If you want to explore the sources, read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the earliest widely available printed version and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s material and Rochdale Borough Council’s site listings for the reserve’s geology, industrial remains and how the folklore is presented to visitors today. The story of the Healey Dwarf is best approached as local folklore — a useful lens on how people in and around Healey have imagined their landscape over two centuries — and as an example of the way place, geology and human storytelling become entangled.

Visiting the Dell remains the most direct way to meet the tradition: the rock alcove, the Thrutch, the viaduct and the heritage displays are all real; the dwarf lives in the stories people tell there.
