articles.title: Ten years without answers: the continuing search for Rochdale’s Jack Stewart
articles.excerpt: Jack Stewart vanished from Spotland on 8 February 2016. His missing-person appeal remains listed a decade later. Here are the original clothing details, what the community did, and how to report information safely.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Daily | Missing persons appeal | 12 October 2026

Ten years after Jack Stewart disappeared from Spotland, a national missing-person charity continues to carry his photograph and an appeal for information. Jack was last reported seen at about 8am on Monday 8 February 2016, at his home on Ings Lane in Rochdale. What happened next remains unknown in the public appeal. For anyone who remembers that morning, or who notices something potentially significant while walking in the area, information can still be passed directly to the police.

Jack's appeal is currently listed by the independent charity Missing People, with reference 16-000774. The charity records him as 68 when he went missing; some original police reporting described him as 69. The important details are the date, location and identifying information, rather than trying to resolve that inconsistency without original records.

Official Missing People appeal: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774

THE MORNING JACK WAS LAST SEEN

At around 8am on Monday 8 February 2016, Jack was seen at his home on Ings Lane, Spotland. Police said his disappearance was extremely out of character, noting that he liked routine in his life. That detail matters because those familiar with his everyday movements may be able to distinguish an ordinary journey from a change in habit. The information available publicly does not establish which direction he travelled, what happened after 8am or why he disappeared.

Contemporary reports describe Jack as a white man, approximately 5ft 9in tall, with brown-and-grey hair worn in a distinctive 'teddy boy' style. His clothing was described in early coverage as a BLACK QUILTED JACKET, BLACK JEANS, STRIPED SOCKS and a DARK-COLOURED CHECK SHIRT. These are the last publicly reported clothing details, not proof that any item would remain recognisable today. Colours, fabrics and descriptions may change over time. The police are best placed to assess the significance of any discovery.

Sources: original 2016 Greater Manchester Police appeal, reproduced in subsequent MEN coverage https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/police-new-appeal-over-missing-10871344; later account with clothing description https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas; charity appeal https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774

HOW ROCHDALE RESPONDED

Local people helped to look for Jack soon after he disappeared. Later reporting records that around 60 members of the public joined a search organised from Brotherod Community Centre, near his home. The response reflected a community unwilling to let a neighbour vanish without notice. Those efforts did not produce a publicly confirmed resolution in the records reviewed for this report.

Source: Manchester Evening News coverage of historic missing Greater Manchester residents https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas

JACK AS A PERSON, NOT JUST A MISSING PERSON

Jack was known to police as someone who valued routine. That is one small glimpse of the life behind the appeal: a man whose ordinary day was sufficiently familiar that his absence immediately stood out. Rochdale Daily has not been able to verify specific hobbies, employment history, or details about a wife, partner, children or surviving relatives from reliable public sources. We will not speculate about them or print supposed family memories without permission.

Anyone close to Jack who wishes to share family-approved memories of his interests, favourite places, the things that made him laugh or his daily routine may contact the newsroom. There is no expectation that relatives should speak publicly. Their privacy and wellbeing come first, and the missing-person appeal does not require the family to relive events for others' curiosity.

TEN YEARS ON: NO CONCLUSIONS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

Jack's continued listing on Missing People means the public appeal has not been withdrawn on the charity's site at the time of this report. It does not establish that he died, that he was harmed by another person, or that the police are pursuing any particular theory. The precise investigative status, searches undertaken since 2016 and any new leads have not been confirmed in a current statement from Greater Manchester Police.

A decade passing does not turn an unverified theory into fact. Whether someone remembers a sighting, has a dated photograph or recalls an unusual circumstance, even a detail that seemed insignificant at the time may be worth submitting to the officers responsible.

IF YOU ARE WALKING YOUR DOG AND FIND SOMETHING CONCERNING

If you come across clothing, personal effects, bones or other material that might be connected to a missing-person case, DO NOT try to decide yourself whether it belongs to Jack. Many items will have entirely unrelated explanations.

If you suspect you have found human remains or a scene requiring an urgent police response, call 999. Do not touch, move, uncover, collect or take anything home; do not dig or disturb the surrounding ground. Keep children and dogs away and avoid walking through the immediate area. Move to a safe position, note the location using a nearby landmark or phone map pin if it is safe to do so, and wait for police instructions.

For a non-urgent recollection, possible sighting or information about the 2016 disappearance, contact Greater Manchester Police on 101 or via https://www.gmp.police.uk. Tell the operator this concerns Jack Stewart, missing from Spotland on 8 February 2016, and provide the Missing People reference 16-000774 as an identifying aid. A charity reference is not necessarily a police incident number.

Please do not post photographs of potentially sensitive evidence, suspected remains, or unverified names online. Do not organise an unsupervised search of private land, woodland or waterways. Any possible discovery should go straight to police, who can preserve and assess evidence and contact families appropriately.

General official guidance on missing-person sightings and reporting: https://www.gov.uk/report-missing-person; UK Missing Persons Unit: https://www.nationalcrimeagency.gov.uk/missingpersons

WHAT IF YOU SIMPLY REMEMBER SOMETHING?

People who lived or worked around Ings Lane, Spotland or neighbouring areas in February 2016 might remember a morning journey, conversation or circumstance that they never associated with the disappearance. You do not need to be certain that a memory is significant before discussing it with police. Explain how confident you are, distinguish what you personally saw from what someone else told you, and do not guess to fill gaps.

The charity Missing People also accepts information confidentially. Call or text 116 000, or use the 'Report a sighting' link at https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774. Contacting the charity should not delay a call to police where there is an immediate danger or potential crime scene.

HELP FOR FAMILIES, FRIENDS AND ANYONE AFFECTED

The experience of an unresolved disappearance can affect loved ones and entire communities for years. Missing People offers free, confidential practical and emotional support to relatives, friends and people who are missing themselves. Call or text 116 000. Its family support team can also be reached at family.support@missingpeople.org.uk. Its helpline website lists current operating hours.

Missing People family help: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/get-help/help-services/family-support; helpline: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/get-help/helpline. If you are distressed by something you have encountered, the police or an appropriate health professional can advise on immediate support; Samaritans offers someone to talk to at any hour on 116 123.

ANY INFORMATION MAY MATTER

Jack Stewart was last seen in Rochdale on 8 February 2016. The clothing described in early appeals — a black quilted jacket, black jeans, striped socks and a dark check shirt — remains a potentially useful historical reference, but identification is the responsibility of trained police and forensic professionals.

For his loved ones, what matters is not speculation but a reliable answer. Ten years later, anyone with real information can still help by passing it to the right people. Rochdale Daily invites Greater Manchester Police and Jack's family, if they wish, to provide any verified updated details for a correction or follow-up; no family member is being asked to take part publicly.

articles.title: Rochdale Pioneers Museum hosts archive sessions on local folklore
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will hold free drop-in sessions this weekend, exploring traditional and supernatural tales from the borough's archives, led by Mitch Robinson.
articles.content_html:
The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will host free archive creative drop-in sessions this weekend, focusing on traditional, unusual, and even supernatural tales from the borough's archives. The sessions, led by Mitch Robinson, aim to uncover hidden stories and records, ranging from folklore to magical narratives.

Scheduled for Saturday, October 15, the hour-long sessions will take place at 12.30pm and 2pm, with no prior booking required. Participants will have the opportunity to engage with old books, documents, and letters that often remain stored away, providing a unique insight into the area's history.

The Co-op Heritage Trust, which is facilitating the event, encourages anyone interested in storytelling, history, or creativity to attend. The sessions are particularly suitable for families with older children, as they will delve into themes of folk belief, magic, and the supernatural.

This initiative is part of the 'Open with Care!' programme, designed to inspire and engage the community during the spooky season. Attendees can expect a creative and thought-provoking experience, whether they are history enthusiasts or simply looking for an intriguing activity this weekend.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.summary: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.body:
Anyone from Rochdale who’s ever limped away from a small mishap will recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” For many locals, cruckle means the particular half‑twist or awkward roll of the foot you can often walk off — not a full sprain but a sudden wobble that makes you wince. This usage is recorded in contemporary perceptual descriptions of Greater Manchester speech and has been listed by residents when describing Rochdale’s spoken character. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

The word itself, however, has deeper roots. Historical dialect lexicography gives us a family of related forms — crookle, crukle, cruggle, krukel — all clustered around meanings such as to bend, make crooked, stoop, huddle or hobble. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect sources and Scottish dialect records preserve these cognates, showing the same phonetic shape and similar senses across northern English and Scots varieties. In the Dictionary of the Scots Language you can see cognate entries (kruggle / cruggle / cruckle) used with senses like “to crouch or huddle,” and nineteenth‑century dialect glosses list crookle with senses such as “to make crooked; to bend, twist.” ([dsl.ac.uk](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd00075099))

How did a general sense of bending or crookedness come to mean the small ankle‑roll in Rochdale? Linguists point to ordinary, well‑attested word‑formation processes. A crook/crook‑ family root (suggesting bending, hooking or crookedness) plus a frequentative or diminutive ‑le ending can produce verbs that describe small, repeated, or imitative actions — crook → crookle. Comparable northern and Germanic dialect forms show similar semantic shifts from ‘bend’ or ‘stoop’ toward senses connected with awkward gait or limping; the broader comparative work on Germanic dialect vocabularies helps explain why these forms and meanings sit together. In short, cruckle is linguistically predictable as a local survival and narrowing of an older dialect verb family. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/be/The_semantic_development_of_words_for_%22walk%2C_run%22_in_the_Germanic_languages_%28IA_semanticdevelopm00ihririch%29.pdf))

Is cruckle uniquely Rochdalian? The short answer is: socially, yes — geographically, not absolutely. Perceptual dialect research carried out in Greater Manchester (2024) collected people’s mental maps and comments about local speech; among the keywords used to evoke Rochdale speech were “broad,” “flat,” “guinnel” and “cruckle,” showing that residents and neighbours associate the word particularly with Rochdale. That kind of folk‑linguistic visibility gives a strong local identity to a word even when related forms appear in older records elsewhere. At the same time, historical dictionaries and place‑name evidence show related spellings and senses across northern England and Scotland, so it would be misleading to claim the sound‑type has never occurred outside the area. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Large projects that collect lived speech and crowd‑sourced dialect entries also help explain how such words persist. When the British Library and other public call‑outs gathered regional words, contributors highlighted locally specific items that researchers had not always recorded in older printed dialect dictionaries; popular reportage of that work singled out “cruckle” as an example of a recognisably local term with onomatopoeic appeal. These crowdsourced attestations, together with formal perceptual surveys, are why small words like cruckle keep turning up in contemporary studies of regional identity. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? Cruckle matters because it shows how vocabulary anchors place: the word’s form and original sense are old and shared across northern dialects, but memory, everyday use and local attitude have made it feel distinctly Rochdale. Linguists view it as a useful data point — for historical contact between Lancashire and Yorkshire varieties, for small‑scale semantic narrowing, and for how people use language to say where they’re from. If you’ve got family pronunciations, old spellings or written examples from letters, keep them — local archives and dialect projects welcome material that helps trace exactly when and where words like cruckle shifted meaning and stuck to a place.

Historical dialect lexicography gives us a family of related forms — crookle, crukle, cruggle, krukel — all clustered around meanings such as to bend, make crooked, stoop, huddle or hobble. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect sources and Scottish dialect records preserve these cognates, showing the same phonetic shape and similar senses across northern English and Scots varieties. In the Dictionary of the Scots Language you can see cognate entries (kruggle / cruggle / cruckle) used with senses like “to crouch or huddle,” and nineteenth‑century dialect glosses list crookle with senses such as “to make crooked; to bend, twist.” ([dsl.ac.uk](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd00075099))

How did a general sense of bending or crookedness come to mean the small ankle‑roll in Rochdale? Linguists point to ordinary, well‑attested word‑formation processes. A crook/crook‑ family root (suggesting bending, hooking or crookedness) plus a frequentative or diminutive ‑le ending can produce verbs that describe small, repeated, or imitative actions — crook → crookle. Comparable northern and Germanic dialect forms show similar semantic shifts from ‘bend’ or ‘stoop’ toward senses connected with awkward gait or limping; the broader comparative work on Germanic dialect vocabularies helps explain why these forms and meanings sit together. In short, cruckle is linguistically predictable as a local survival and narrowing of an older dialect verb family. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/be/The_semantic_development_of_words_for_%22walk%2C_run%22_in_the_Germanic_languages_%28IA_semanticdevelopm00ihririch%29.pdf))

Is cruckle uniquely Rochdalian? The short answer is: socially, yes — geographically, not absolutely. Perceptual dialect research carried out in Greater Manchester (2024) collected people’s mental maps and comments about local speech; among the keywords used to evoke Rochdale speech were “broad,” “flat,” “guinnel” and “cruckle,” showing that residents and neighbours associate the word particularly with Rochdale. That kind of folk‑linguistic visibility gives a strong local identity to a word even when related forms appear in older records elsewhere. At the same time, historical dictionaries and place‑name evidence show related spellings and senses across northern England and Scotland, so it would be misleading to claim the sound‑type has never occurred outside the area. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Large projects that collect lived speech and crowd‑sourced dialect entries also help explain how such words persist. When the British Library and other public call‑outs gathered regional words, contributors highlighted locally specific items that researchers had not always recorded in older printed dialect dictionaries; popular reportage of that work singled out “cruckle” as an example of a recognisably local term with onomatopoeic appeal. These crowdsourced attestations, together with formal perceptual surveys, are why small words like cruckle keep turning up in contemporary studies of regional identity. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? Cruckle matters because it shows how vocabulary anchors place: the word’s form and original sense are old and shared across northern dialects, but memory, everyday use and local attitude have made it feel distinctly Rochdale. Linguists view it as a useful data point — for historical contact between Lancashire and Yorkshire varieties, for small‑scale semantic narrowing, and for how people use language to say where they’re from. If you’ve got family pronunciations, old spellings or written examples from letters, keep them — local archives and dialect projects welcome material that helps trace exactly when and where words like cruckle shifted meaning and stuck to a place.

articles.title: Did Robin Hood really come to Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
articles.summary: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
articles.body:
There is a pulpit-shaped rock, a narrow pool and a name — the Fairy Chapel — at the base of Healey Dell’s steep gorge. The visitor centre and local heritage guides record a set of vivid stories: a King of the Fairies who turned a coven to stone, a ring lost in the river that cost a would‑be heir his title, and an origin tale that sends “Robert of Huntingdon” on the road to becoming Robin Hood. These versions are the ones you’ll see on site interpretation and in the Heritage Centre’s write‑ups. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

That is folklore, not archival evidence. The most systematic scholarly account of the Dell is an archaeological desk‑based assessment carried out for Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council by the University of Manchester Archaeological Unit in December 2004. It maps the valley’s mills, lodges, railway viaduct and later Victorian and industrial remains; it lists the local archives and printed sources consulted (John Rylands, Lancashire Record Office, Rochdale Local Studies and others) and documents the Dell’s long industrial and landscape history — but it does not produce contemporary medieval records linking a historical Robin Hood or a Robert of Huntingdon to Healey Dell. Put bluntly: the detailed desk‑based study records place, industry and later antiquarian interest, not a medieval outlaw’s itinerary. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

Healey Dell’s real, verifiable past is useful and interesting in itself. The site is a designated local nature reserve and a managed visitor attraction, with a Victorian railway viaduct that is Grade II listed and the valley’s surviving mill archaeology. Rochdale Borough Council describes the reserve, the visitor centre’s pictorial displays and the family‑oriented Fairy Grotto as part of the attraction visitors can find at Dell Road, Healey. The viaduct and the visible industrial remains are the kinds of things that the archaeological assessment and Historic England record in statutory listings. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

How did the Robin Hood story arrive here? Local legends often accrete around striking landscape features; caverns, pools and ravines attract tales of fairies, witches and enchanted tokens across Britain. The Healey Dell accounts appear in local storytelling and modern retellings by the Heritage Centre and local guides: they make no claim to derive from contemporary medieval documents but preserve a late tradition tying a Huntingdon name and a lost ring to the Chapel. Those popular accounts are part of the Dell’s cultural history and of local imaginative life — important for tourism and local identity — but they do not equal documentary proof. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

On the bigger question of Robin Hood’s historicity, mainstream scholarship treats Robin Hood as a legendary figure built from ballads and popular tales rather than a single, verifiable medieval person whose movements can be read off local court rolls. Modern reference works and folklorists stress the ballad tradition and its late medieval and post‑medieval formation; many local Robin Hood claims around England are later inventions, popular attributions or imaginative explanations for landscape oddities rather than recordable events. That does not make the stories worthless — it makes them folklore. ([books.google.com](https://books.google.com/books/about/Oxford_Dictionary_of_English_Folklore.html?hl=en&id=w2BMSAAACAAJ&output=html_text))

So what can a reader reasonably take away? If you mean “is there documentary, contemporary medieval evidence that Robin Hood or Robert of Huntingdon passed through Healey Dell?” the answer is: no such evidence has been produced in the local archival and archaeological surveys cited by the University of Manchester assessment and by the council’s heritage material. If you mean “are there stories that people tell about Robin Hood, witches and a magic ring here?” the answer is yes — they are recorded in local guides and on site interpretation, and they help make the place culturally lively. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

If you want to read more or check sources yourself: the University of Manchester archaeological desk‑based assessment (2004) is the most thorough published study of Healey Dell’s historic fabric; Rochdale Borough Council holds the reserve’s visitor information; the Healey Dell Heritage Centre publishes the Fairy Chapel story used in interpretation. None of these sources substitutes for a named medieval document placing Robin Hood in the Dell — and until such a record appears, the Robin Hood connection belongs to folklore rather than local history. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

articles.title: Heywood Army Cadet Detachment opens its doors for National Cadets Week
articles.excerpt: Heywood Army Cadet Detachment is inviting young people and their parents or carers to an open evening on Thursday 8 October to discover what the Army Cadets has to offer.
articles.content_html:
Heywood Army Cadet Detachment is opening its doors as part of National Cadets Week, inviting young people and their parents or carers to come along and find out more about the Army Cadets.

The open evening will take place on Thursday 8 October from 7pm to 8.30pm at Heywood Detachment on Bamford Road, Heywood, OL10 4FT.

Visitors will be able to meet instructors and cadets, look around the detachment and find out more about activities available through the Army Cadets.

The programme can include adventure, fieldcraft, shooting, first aid, sport, the Duke of Edinburgh's Award, camps and leadership opportunities, as well as the chance to make new friends and try something different.

The detachment says no military experience is needed and that the open evening is an opportunity to see what Army Cadets is about and where participation could lead.

Young people and their parents or carers are invited to attend.

articles.excerpt: Christ Church Healey will hold its Harvest service on 18 October, followed by a special afternoon service to bless the church bells with the Rt Rev'd Bishop Mark.
articles.content_html:
Christ Church Healey will hold its Harvest celebration on Sunday 18 October, with the church also welcoming the Rt Rev'd Bishop Mark for a special service to bless its bells later the same day.

The Harvest service begins at 10am. The church is asking those attending to bring donations of non-perishable food, which will be given to the food bank.

A second service will take place at 2pm, when the Rt Rev'd Bishop Mark will join the congregation for a special service to bless the bells.

The bell-blessing service will be followed by light refreshments in the church hall.

Christ Church Healey is inviting members of the local community to join both services and take part in the day's celebrations.

articles.title: Remembrance and reflection walks offer bereaved service families a place to connect at Denehurst Park
articles.excerpt: Get Together After Serving CIC invites families, partners and loved ones to a gentle weekly remembrance walk at Denehurst Park in Rochdale, with no pressure to talk about loss.
articles.content_html:
A weekly remembrance walk in Rochdale is offering families and loved ones of fallen service personnel a chance to find companionship, fresh air and a little space to reflect.

Organised by Get Together After Serving CIC (G.A.S-CIC), the Remembrance & Reflection Walk takes place every Wednesday at Denehurst Park. Participants are invited to meet outside Denehurst Café at 12.30pm before setting off together.

The gentle walk is expected to last between 30 minutes and an hour, depending on the weather. Dogs are very welcome, although there is no need to bring one to take part.

At the heart of the initiative is the understanding that grief does not always need words. Those attending can share memories of someone they have lost, chat about everyday life, walk quietly or simply enjoy being in the company of people who understand.

The event poster captures that sentiment: “Sometimes you don’t need a meeting or a support group. Sometimes you just need to get outside, walk, talk and spend some time with people who understand.”

After the walk, the group plans to return to Denehurst Café for a warm drink, a slice of cake and more time together for anyone who wishes to stay.

The invitation is aimed at families and loved ones remembering fallen heroes, with partners and friends also welcome. There is no expectation to discuss personal experiences or bereavement, and those who would prefer a quiet walk will be just as welcome as those looking for conversation.

The weekly gathering brings remembrance into the everyday: not only formal ceremonies or anniversaries, but a simple opportunity to come together, one Wednesday at a time.

Walk details: Every Wednesday at 12.30pm. Meeting point: outside Denehurst Café, Denehurst Park, Rochdale. The walk lasts 30 minutes to one hour, weather permitting. Dogs are welcome, but are not required. Participants can return to the café afterwards for optional refreshments and company.

articles.title: Rochdale’s Breaking Barriers secures core funding to expand its cultural work across Greater Manchester
articles.excerpt: Rochdale-based production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of GMCA core funding to expand cultural programmes, paid opportunities and creative development across Greater Manchester.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale-based multidisciplinary production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of core funding from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to strengthen the organisation and expand its cultural programmes across the region.

Over the funding period, Breaking Barriers plans to offer 42 paid placements through its Young Company programme, giving creatives aged 18–25 hands-on experience working on professional arts productions.

It will also provide 328 paid freelance roles and 45 in-kind artist residencies at its Rochdale base at Richard Street Studios.

Young Company participants will gain practical skills in producing, sound design, filmmaking and direction, with a focus on young people from underrepresented backgrounds who have had fewer opportunities to get into the arts.

A producer development programme will also support 36 creative producers a year to develop their own projects, secure resources and build sustainable careers.

Awarded through the Spirit strand of the GMCA Culture Fund, the investment will support Breaking Barriers to continue delivering theatre, film and immersive outdoor artworks, alongside training, mentoring and paid opportunities for emerging creatives.

Parvez Qadir, Artistic Director of Breaking Barriers, said: “Three years of core funding gives us the stability to plan ahead and grow as a company here in Rochdale. There’s so much creative talent locally, and we can now give more young people paid opportunities to work alongside experienced artists on our productions. It also enables us to keep building partnerships across Greater Manchester and develop projects shaped by local people, bringing their stories to life.”

Bev Craig, Mayor of Greater Manchester, said: “Culture has the power to connect communities, inspire creativity and strengthen pride in the places we call home.

“Through the Greater Manchester Culture Fund, we're investing in a diverse range of cultural organisations that help make our city region such a vibrant and inclusive place to live. Breaking Barriers is a fantastic example of a local company creating opportunities for young people to share their stories, develop their creativity and shape cultural experiences on their doorstep.”

Projects are currently planned to span the boroughs of Rochdale, Bury, Salford, Stockport, Manchester, Tameside and Bolton over three years.

Residents and local communities will help create outdoor artworks using sound, projection and light, alongside films and digital storytelling projects reflecting local experiences.

The funding will also help sustain and expand Breaking Barriers’ theatre in education work.

This includes multi-partnership delivery of Crossing the Line, a theatre and workshop programme tackling child criminal exploitation, which has already reached more than 15,000 young people across more than 220 schools.

Blind Side, exploring violence against women and girls, consent and healthy relationships, will continue to tour. Support from the Spirit strand will enable more time and resources to further expand its reach into other boroughs.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway wins Community Hero Award for its volunteers
articles.excerpt: East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.
articles.content_html:
East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.

The awards celebrate people, groups, charities and businesses that go the extra mile to support others and strengthen their communities. The railway said the recognition reflects the commitment of its volunteers and the role the heritage line continues to play across the communities it serves.

The East Lancashire Railway operates heritage trains through the Irwell Valley, connecting communities including Bury, Summerseat, Ramsbottom, Irwell Vale, Rawtenstall and Heywood.

Diesel Driver and Head of the Signalling Department Linda Henderson said the railway could not exist without its volunteers.

"For almost 40 years, the ELR has operated Heritage trains through the heart of the Irwell Valley. Without volunteers, the ELR and Heritage Railways throughout the UK would not exist."

Henderson said the award recognised more than 800 current volunteers as well as those who had previously given their time to the railway.

Chairman Mike Kelly said he was "extremely proud" to accept the award on behalf of the railway and its volunteers, describing their work as generous and unselfish.

Kelly, who is also a volunteer, said the recognition highlighted the commitment and passion volunteers bring to organisations across local communities. He also thanked Roch Valley Radio for recognising volunteers and the contribution they make to charities and community organisations.

The award was collected by a group of volunteers representing several parts of the railway, including train operations, signalling, the guards department, the dining train team and a station café.

The East Lancashire Railway said the award was a recognition of the hard work and continued dedication of all its volunteers.

articles.title: Rochdale Sleepout 2026 returns to raise funds and awareness for people facing homelessness
articles.excerpt: Petrus is calling on Rochdale residents, businesses and community groups to get behind Rochdale Sleepout 2026 and help raise vital funds for local people experiencing homelessness and social exclusion.
articles.content_html:
Petrus Community is calling on people across Rochdale to get behind Rochdale Sleepout 2026, a fundraising and awareness event designed to highlight the realities faced by people experiencing homelessness while raising vital funds for local support services.

The Rochdale-based charity supports people experiencing homelessness, poverty and social exclusion across the borough. The Sleepout challenges participants to spend a night outdoors while learning more about homelessness and the support available locally.

Organisers are keen to stress that the event is not intended to replicate the experience of homelessness. Instead, it aims to encourage conversation, build understanding and raise money to support people accessing Petrus services.

Last year's inaugural Rochdale Sleepout brought supporters together from across the borough and raised £7,875.52 for Rochdale AFC Community Trust and Petrus.

The money raised has already helped launch Changing Lives, a partnership supporting people experiencing homelessness and those living in supported accommodation through football, wellbeing, education and employability opportunities.

According to Petrus, participants involved in the programme are rebuilding confidence, making new friendships, developing new skills and becoming more active members of their communities.

This year's event is also an opportunity for local businesses, community groups and individuals to get involved by taking part, sponsoring participants or making a donation.

Funds raised through the Sleepout will support Petrus' work across Rochdale, including homelessness prevention, housing support, wellbeing services, education and training opportunities, and practical support for some of the borough's most vulnerable residents.

Petrus is encouraging anyone interested in supporting the event to help spread the word and get involved.

articles.excerpt: Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers are taking on a 45-mile charity walk on Saturday, 31 October, to raise money for four causes close to their hearts.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers are swapping the rugby pitch for the road as members of the groups prepare to take on a 45-mile charity walk on Saturday, 31 October.

The challenge is being organised to raise as much money as possible for four causes close to the participants' hearts: Springhill Hospice, the Motor Neurone Disease Association (MND), Rochdale Masters and Rugby League Cares.

Organisers are expecting the walk to be a major physical challenge, but say they want it to become about more than completing 45 miles. They are also appealing to local businesses and members of the community to get behind the fundraising effort.

Businesses are being encouraged to support the challenge through sponsorship, donations, supplies for the day or simply by sharing the fundraiser with customers, colleagues and their wider networks.

The organisers said: "We're not playing rugby for this one… we're putting the boots down and walking 45 miles!"

The group hopes that local support will help raise as much money as possible for the four causes while bringing businesses, sports communities and residents together around the challenge.

Anyone who can help with sponsorship, donations, supplies or promotion is encouraged to get in touch with the organisers.

Mandy from Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers said the group would be happy to provide photographs, route details and further information about the charities involved, as well as speak about the challenge.

articles.title: Oliver Coldman crowned champion golfer at Rochdale Golf Club Captain’s Final
articles.excerpt: Oliver Coldman has won Rochdale Golf Club’s 2026 Captain’s Final with a two-round total of 133, four shots ahead of runner-up Steve Royle.
articles.content_html:
Oliver Coldman has been crowned Rochdale Golf Club’s Champion Golfer for 2026 after winning the Captain’s Final during a weekend of competition at the club.

Coldman recorded rounds of 69 and 64 for a combined score of 133 to take the Captain’s Final title. Steve Royle finished runner-up after rounds of 67 and 70 gave him a total of 137.

The weekend also saw a series of other prizes decided. Raymond Clegg claimed Best Nett on Saturday, while Tom Wilson took Best Nett on Sunday.

Aaron Buckley won the Darren Ogden Memorial Trophy, awarded for nearest the pin in two on the 18th, with a distance of 2.13 metres. Steve George was named the lowest qualifier at 10 under par.

Rochdale Golf Club said the weekend had produced some brilliant golf despite the threat of rain, and congratulated all of the finalists and winners. The club also thanked the volunteers and staff involved in staging what it described as a special annual event.

A charity raffle was drawn during the weekend, with the club thanking supporters who bought tickets as well as the donors who supplied prizes. A full list of raffle prize winners is expected to be emailed to members over the coming days.

The Captain’s Final is one of the highlights of the club calendar, bringing together qualifiers for the concluding competition and recognising performances across the weekend.

articles.title: Homelessness, addiction and the cruelty of public condemnation
articles.excerpt: A disabled homeless man outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road has become the subject of photographs, insults and jokes online. The harder question is whether public humiliation solves anything at all.
articles.content_html:
There is a homeless man who regularly sits outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road in Rochdale. He uses a wheelchair, has one leg, and appears to have longstanding problems with drug dependency. In recent days, photographs purporting to show him using drugs have been circulated in a local social-media group, accompanied by descriptions including ‘junkie’, ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’, together with jokes about his disability.

Those comments deserve more scrutiny than the man they were aimed at.

It is entirely legitimate for residents to object to public drug use, theft, abusive behaviour or intimidation. It is legitimate for shop workers to expect protection at work. It is legitimate for parents to dislike exposing children to distressing scenes. But there is a clear moral distinction between criticising behaviour and publicly degrading a vulnerable person. Calling a homeless, disabled man a ‘scruff’ does not protect children. Making jokes about his missing leg does not reduce drug use. Posting photographs of him at what may be one of the lowest points of his life does not help shop staff, improve public safety or increase the likelihood that he enters treatment. It serves a different purpose: humiliation.

The ease with which some people have participated in that humiliation should trouble us.

The editor of Rochdale Daily has spoken to this man several times. In those encounters, he has not demanded money. He has generally asked for a drink, usually a chocolate milkshake. Other residents have independently described similar experiences. A Tesco worker has, by contrast, said that staff sometimes experience him as abusive. Both accounts may be true. Addiction, withdrawal, mental distress and homelessness do not produce consistent behaviour.

That does not make abuse acceptable. But neither does difficult behaviour grant the public permission to strip somebody of dignity.

During one conversation, the man said he had previously been prescribed methadone but stopped collecting it because he felt demeaned and discriminated against when attending the dispensing pharmacy. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that account. When asked whether he would consider restarting treatment if his medication could be dispensed somewhere he felt able to attend, he said yes.

That exchange should matter more than a photograph. It suggests that beneath the visible disorder is a person who can still discuss treatment, medication and the possibility of changing his circumstances. Yet this is precisely the sort of person whom public discussion can rapidly reduce to a caricature. Once the word ‘junkie’ has been applied, the individual disappears and only the label remains. That is not analysis. It is intellectual laziness.

Addiction is not a mysterious condition. It is extensively studied, medically recognised and strongly associated with homelessness, trauma, mental ill-health and social exclusion. National treatment statistics show that among people entering treatment for opiate problems in England in 2024–25, 41 per cent had no home of their own and 10 per cent were sleeping rough. Government research into rough sleeping published in 2025 found that 54 per cent of respondents reported a drug or alcohol misuse need during the preceding year.

These figures do not excuse criminal or antisocial behaviour. They do, however, make a mockery of the idea that addiction can be solved by simply telling somebody to ‘sort themselves out’. A person who is homeless must try to recover without privacy, stability, reliable sleep, secure storage, regular meals or often even basic hygiene. They may need to attend treatment, collect prescriptions, keep appointments, manage benefits, maintain identification documents and navigate housing applications while sleeping outside. To describe failure under those conditions as proof of moral inferiority is not toughness. It is ignorance.

One comment in the local discussion suggested that drug users should do these things ‘behind their own doors’. That statement is revealing precisely because the man in question does not have one.

Most people have the privilege of experiencing their worst behaviour privately. They can drink too much behind curtains, suffer mental-health crises in bedrooms, argue with family in kitchens, withdraw from medication under a duvet or make disastrous decisions without a stranger photographing them. A rough sleeper does not have a private sphere. His bedroom is public. His living room is public. His breakdowns are public. His addiction is public. And then the same society that has left him without a private space condemns him for failing to keep his problems out of sight. There is something deeply incoherent about that.

The man's disability makes the tone of some comments particularly ugly. Government research published in 2025 found that 80 per cent of people surveyed while sleeping rough reported a longstanding physical impairment, illness or disability. Yet a local discussion about a homeless man with one leg included jokes about his wheelchair. There is no serious public-interest argument for that. It is not community safety. It is not concern for children. It is not anger about shoplifting. It is mockery of disability, and adults should be capable of naming that for what it is.

The same applies to language such as ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’. Such terms do not describe conduct; they reduce a person to a social category deemed beneath respect. The implication is that once somebody becomes sufficiently poor, addicted or visibly disordered, ordinary standards of human decency no longer apply to the way we speak about them. That proposition should be rejected. A person's entitlement to dignity cannot depend upon whether they are pleasant enough, clean enough, sober enough or useful enough to satisfy strangers on Facebook.

Rochdale also needs to confront the practical context. The borough is already under intense housing pressure. Under Places for Everyone, Rochdale's housing requirement for 2025 to 2030 is 616 homes per year. Council material from 2025 recorded 7,681 applicants on the housing register, while more recent council reporting has referred to approximately 20,000 people relying upon the register and nearly 7,500 meeting statutory ‘reasonable preference’ criteria. Rochdale Council declared a housing emergency in 2023.

So the instruction often directed at people like this man is effectively the following: become sober, become stable, engage with treatment, organise your paperwork, maintain appointments, secure benefits and compete for scarce housing, all while sleeping outside and managing a major physical disability. That is not impossible. But anyone describing it as simple has probably never attempted anything remotely comparable.

There are also legal considerations when photographs and allegations are published online. Taking a photograph in a public place is not automatically unlawful, and Rochdale Daily is not suggesting otherwise. Identifiable images can, depending on context, constitute personal data, while publishing a photograph alongside a serious allegation of criminal behaviour raises separate legal questions.

The Defamation Act 2013 provides protection against statements that cause or are likely to cause serious reputational harm. Truth may be a defence, but that is different from saying that anything alleged on social media is lawful merely because the publisher believes it. If an identifiable photograph is accompanied by an assertion that a person is committing a criminal offence, the publisher should be in a position to substantiate what is being alleged. Rochdale Daily is therefore not independently stating that the man was consuming a Class A drug based solely on photographs and comments circulated online.

There is an additional point that some contributors may wish to consider before reaching for the camera. Vulnerability does not make somebody public property. The fact that a person's suffering occurs on a pavement does not create an entitlement to turn it into entertainment, gossip or a community spectacle. There may be circumstances in which photographing suspected criminal behaviour serves a legitimate evidential purpose. There is a substantial difference between preserving evidence for police and distributing an image among neighbours so that strangers can compete to produce the most contemptuous description of the person depicted. One is potentially evidence gathering. The other can become a form of public shaming.

And public shaming has a cost. If a person already believes that institutions regard him as worthless, if he already feels humiliated collecting treatment, if strangers photograph him and hundreds of neighbours discuss whether he is a ‘scruff’, then it should not surprise anyone if disengagement, isolation and further drug use follow. People sometimes ask why addicts do not seek help while simultaneously creating a social environment in which admitting addiction results in contempt. They demand recovery while reinforcing shame. They demand engagement while making the person feel despised. They demand that somebody rejoin society while making it clear that society would rather not look at them. Those positions are difficult to reconcile.

There is also a tendency to present compassion as naïveté. Those who have defended the man have been dismissed as ‘Karens’ or ‘do gooders’, as though refusing to join in public degradation demonstrates some failure to understand the realities of addiction. The opposite may be true. It requires very little sophistication to dislike someone behaving badly in public. It requires considerably more maturity to condemn the behaviour without enjoying the destruction of the person.

Compassion does not mean giving unlimited money to somebody with an addiction. It does not mean ignoring theft. It does not mean expecting retail workers to endure abuse. It does not mean pretending crack cocaine is harmless. It means retaining the ability to distinguish a human being from his worst behaviour. That distinction is central to every serious approach to rehabilitation.

If society genuinely wants people to recover from addiction, then those people must eventually be able to imagine themselves as something other than an addict. If every interaction reinforces that they are disgusting, worthless and permanently defined by their dependency, society should not be surprised when they behave as though there is little left to recover.

Rochdale Council lists homelessness support, drug and alcohol treatment and specialist services including Turning Point. Those services are important, but complex cases require coordination. A homeless person with a major physical disability and drug dependency may simultaneously require healthcare, treatment, medication management, benefits assistance, housing support and persistent outreach. That is difficult work. Writing ‘absolute scruff’ beneath a photograph is considerably easier. Perhaps that is part of its appeal. It allows people to experience the satisfaction of condemning a social problem without undertaking any of the difficult work involved in solving it.

There is a legitimate debate to be had about public drug use in Rochdale. There is a legitimate debate about homelessness, shoplifting, antisocial behaviour, policing, treatment capacity and the availability of supported accommodation. Those are serious subjects. Wheelchair jokes are not. Photographing a visibly vulnerable disabled man for the purpose of ridicule is not. Describing somebody at the lowest point of his life as though he were vermin contributes nothing whatsoever to the safety or wellbeing of Rochdale.

Residents are entitled to expect streets that are safe and usable. Tesco staff are entitled to work without abuse. Children should not have to encounter dangerous drug paraphernalia. Police should deal with offences where offences occur. But none of those propositions requires cruelty.

The question for Rochdale is not whether this man is admirable. He may not be. The question is whether a civilised community applies standards of dignity only to people whose lives are already in order. Most of the people commenting about him will eventually put their phones down and return home. They will have a bathroom, a bed, heating, a front door and somewhere to make their mistakes privately. He will still be outside. That difference should produce some humility.

If a community cannot look at a homeless, addicted, disabled man without turning his circumstances into entertainment, then there is more than one social problem on display. One is sitting on the pavement. The other is holding the camera.

articles.title: Rochdale businesses urged to back Denehurst House in £30-a-month veterans challenge
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale veterans support organisation is asking 100 local businesses to pledge £30 a month to help keep Denehurst House operational and support former service personnel in need.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale veterans support organisation has launched a drive to recruit 100 local businesses willing to pledge £30 a month towards keeping Denehurst House operational.

Get Together After Serving CIC, which is behind the campaign, says Denehurst House provides support for veterans including emergency housing, hot meals and mental health support. The organisation is promoting the appeal as the Rochdale 100 Businesses Challenge and is asking firms across the borough to make a regular monthly contribution.

If all 100 places are filled, the campaign would generate £3,000 each month in pledged support, equivalent to £36,000 over a full year if every business remained involved for 12 months. The appeal describes the contribution as a relatively small commitment for an individual business which, collectively, could make a significant difference to the service.

Campaign material highlights community spirit, warm meals and local businesses working together, with the message: 'Together, we keep Denehurst House operational.' It also says the project aims to provide a lifeline to veterans when they need it most.

The initiative is seeking support from companies of all sizes rather than relying on a handful of major donors. That model would spread the cost across the local business community while giving Denehurst House a more predictable stream of recurring income.

Local businesses interested in joining the challenge are being asked to contact Get Together After Serving CIC by emailing hello@gtascic.co.uk.

Rochdale Daily is publishing the appeal as today's front-page community story to help local firms understand what is being requested, how the funding model works and how they can take part.

articles.title: Can’t make it to church? Christ Church Healey invites community to join Sunday service online
articles.excerpt: Christ Church Healey is inviting people who cannot attend in person, are new to church or simply want to find out more to join its Sunday morning service online each week.
articles.content_html:
People across Healey and the wider Rochdale community who are unable to attend church in person are being warmly invited to join Christ Church's Sunday morning service online each week.

The church's weekly livestream is also open to people who may be new to church, curious about Christianity or who would simply feel more comfortable experiencing a service from home before deciding whether to attend in person.

Christ Church goes live at 9.55am every Sunday morning, allowing viewers to watch the service as it happens. Anyone who cannot watch at that time can catch up afterwards, with the service remaining available to view later.

The church said: “You are most welcome to join us for our weekly Sunday morning livestream from Christ Church. You can watch the service live as it happens, or at any time afterwards. We go live at 9.55am.”

For people who are housebound, unwell, caring for somebody, working on Sunday mornings or otherwise unable to be physically present, the livestream provides a way to remain connected with worship and the local church community.

It can also offer a gentle introduction for anyone who has never attended church before. There is no requirement to already be a member of the congregation — viewers can simply tune in from home and see what a Sunday morning at Christ Church is like.

The livestream runs each Sunday, with the broadcast beginning at 9.55am. Christ Church Healey welcomes both its existing congregation and newcomers joining online.

Manuel and Janine from MBF Cleaning met with Ruth at Rochdale Foodbank to discuss the charity's work, share ideas and explore practical ways the business could make a difference.

The foodbank's van plays an important role in day-to-day operations, helping bring in supplies and donations before delivering food parcels to distribution points around Rochdale.

By sponsoring the vehicle, MBF Cleaning is helping the charity maintain that transport link and continue supporting people facing hardship across the borough.

Rochdale Foodbank is also encouraging other local businesses to consider becoming corporate partners. Companies interested in supporting the charity can find more information about partnership opportunities through Rochdale Foodbank's website.

The charity says it would welcome conversations with businesses interested in working together to support the local community.

Janine from MBF Cleaning is pictured with Ruth from Rochdale Foodbank in the original announcement.

articles.title: This week in Rochdale, 100 years ago: the town captured from the air in August 1926
articles.excerpt: Exactly a century ago this month, aerial photographers captured remarkable views of Rochdale's Town Hall, Yorkshire Street, railway station, Broadfield Park and industrial works — preserving the town as it looked in August 1926.
articles.content_html:
One hundred years ago this week, Rochdale was a very different town — but thanks to a remarkable series of aerial photographs taken in August 1926, we can still see it almost street by street.

The images, held by the Britain From Above archive, show a dense industrial town of mills, railway infrastructure, tramways, terraced streets and civic buildings. They provide one of the clearest surviving visual records of Rochdale in the inter-war period.

Yorkshire Street was photographed from the air in August 1926 under reference EPW016788. The view shows the familiar line of the street threading through tightly packed buildings, with factories, chimneys and terraced housing occupying much of the surrounding landscape. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016788

Rochdale railway station was also captured that month under reference EPW016784. The photograph shows not only the station but the extraordinary concentration of railway sidings, engineering works and industrial premises that once surrounded this part of the town. The archive identifies features including railway works, cotton mills, a goods shed and the Rochdale Canal terminal basin. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016784

Another image, EPW016791, looks across Town Hall Square. It records landmarks that remain instantly recognisable alongside features which have since vanished or changed beyond recognition. Archive annotations identify St Chad's, the Esplanade, Rochdale Post Office, Drake Street, tramcars and the Rochdale War Memorial while it was still under construction. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016791

Broadfield Park was photographed in the same month under reference EPW016782, giving another extraordinary perspective across the civic heart of Rochdale. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016782

The industrial scale of the town is perhaps most obvious in the August 1926 photographs of Fishwick Street. Image EPW016789 records the railway works there, reflecting the huge engineering and manufacturing presence which once surrounded Rochdale's rail network. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016789

Even before that August series, an Aerofilms photograph taken on 6 August 1926 captured Rochdale Road crossing the railway and Rochdale Canal at Slattocks. The image, EPW016440, preserves a landscape where canal, railway and road infrastructure sat side by side — the transport arteries which helped power the borough's industrial economy. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016440

What is striking about these photographs is not simply what has disappeared. It is how much remains legible. The Town Hall, St Chad's, major road alignments and parts of the railway landscape allow modern residents to orient themselves inside a town photographed from an aircraft a century ago.

The photographs also capture Rochdale during a period of profound change. The borough remained heavily industrial, public transport still included corporation tramcars, and mills and engineering works dominated huge areas which today contain housing, roads, offices and redeveloped land.

The Rochdale Observer itself was already a long-established part of town life by 1926, having first appeared in 1856. Its surviving archive means future editions of Rochdale Daily's '100 Years Ago' feature can go beyond photographs and recover the stories residents were actually reading — crime reports, council debates, sport, advertisements, court cases, births, deaths and the everyday incidents which made up life in the borough.

For this first edition, though, the photographs tell their own story. They allow us to look down on Rochdale exactly a century ago and recognise both the town we inherited and the one that disappeared.

Rochdale Daily intends to make 'This Week in Rochdale — 100 Years Ago' a recurring history feature throughout the centenary year.

IMAGE NOTE: The historic Aerofilms photographs referenced above are held by Britain From Above. Their terms do not permit commercial reproduction without a separate licence, so Rochdale Daily links readers to the original archive images rather than reproducing them without permission.

articles.title: Little'Pink'borough returns as businesses across Littleborough prepare to turn pink for Cancer Research UK
articles.excerpt: Businesses and organisations across Littleborough, Hollingworth Lake and Wardle are being invited to take part in Little'Pink'borough, a community campaign raising awareness and funds for Cancer Research UK.
articles.content_html:
Littleborough is preparing to turn pink once again as one of the area's colourful community fundraising campaigns returns in eight weeks.

Little'Pink'borough is inviting shops, pubs, clubs, cafés, restaurants, doctors' surgeries, dentists, hairdressers and businesses across Littleborough, Hollingworth Lake and Wardle to get involved in support of Cancer Research UK.

The campaign, organised by The Three Amigos FUNdraising Group, encourages local organisations to create their own pink-themed displays and help transform the area while raising awareness of cancer research.

Businesses are welcome to organise their own fundraising activities as part of the campaign, although organisers stress that in-house fundraising is appreciated rather than essential. Simply taking part and creating a display helps build the community-wide event.

Photographs from previous years are being shared to provide inspiration and get local businesses thinking about what they could create this time around.

There is also a competitive element. The organisation judged to have the best display will receive a bespoke trophy to keep for a year, with the winner's name engraved on it permanently as part of the event's history.

The campaign brings together businesses, community organisations and residents from across the wider Littleborough area around a common cause, while giving streets and shopfronts a distinctive pink makeover.

This year's Little'Pink'borough is being supported by Whittaker Golf Club, which is sponsoring the campaign. The club offers memberships and individual rounds of golf, with further information available through its website.

With eight weeks to go, The Three Amigos FUNdraising Group is encouraging organisations to start planning their displays and decide how they would like to take part.

Further details about the event and fundraising activities are expected as Little'Pink'borough approaches.
articles.right_to_reply: Littleborough, Wardle and Hollingworth Lake businesses taking part in Little'Pink'borough can send photographs, fundraising plans and community updates to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Residents urge dog owners to clean up after pets amid fouling concerns in Milnrow and Newhey
articles.excerpt: Residents in Milnrow and Newhey are calling on dog owners to pick up after their pets following complaints about dog mess being left in public areas, alongside local concern about parvovirus.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Milnrow and Newhey are urging dog owners to take responsibility for cleaning up after their pets following growing frustration about dog fouling in local public areas.

Community members say the amount of dog mess being left behind has become unacceptable, creating an unpleasant problem for pedestrians, families and responsible dog walkers.

The message from residents is straightforward: if your dog fouls in a public place, carry a bag, pick it up and dispose of it properly.

Concerns have also been heightened by reports among local dog owners about canine parvovirus in the area. Parvovirus is a highly contagious viral illness affecting dogs and can be particularly serious for puppies and unvaccinated animals. The virus can be shed in the faeces of infected dogs and can persist in contaminated environments, making good hygiene and responsible disposal of dog waste especially important.

Rochdale Daily has not independently confirmed the extent of any current local parvovirus outbreak, so owners concerned about their dog's health should seek advice from a veterinary professional rather than relying on social-media reports.

Dog fouling is not simply an inconvenience. People should not have to navigate dog mess on pavements, paths, grassed areas and other shared spaces, while responsible owners should not have to worry about their pets walking through waste left behind by somebody else.

Residents are asking owners to remember that responsibility for clearing up belongs to the person in charge of the dog. It should not be left for council workers, other dog walkers or members of the public to deal with.

Picking up takes seconds and helps keep Milnrow and Newhey cleaner and safer for everyone using local streets and green spaces.

The message is simple: carry a bag, pick it up and bin it.

articles.title: New Whitworth venue Lillie's to serve kindness alongside cocktails with 'Be Kind' initiative
articles.excerpt: Guests at Lillie's in Whitworth will find anonymous handwritten messages of encouragement waiting at their tables as part of a new 'Be Kind' initiative designed to spread a little positivity from one visitor to the next.
articles.content_html:
A new Whitworth hospitality venue is planning to put kindness at the heart of its bottomless brunches by passing anonymous handwritten messages of encouragement from one guest to the next.

Lillie's, which is preparing to open in Whitworth, says its ambition has always been to create more than simply somewhere to enjoy cocktails, food and company. Its owner wants customers to leave feeling a little happier than when they arrived.

That idea has now developed into the venue's new 'Be Kind' initiative.

Every guest attending a Bottomless Brunch will be welcomed with a signature Lillie's cocktail and a sealed Be Kind envelope waiting at the table. Inside will be a handwritten message from a previous guest containing words of kindness, encouragement, positivity or support. The messages will be completely anonymous.

Each envelope will also contain a fresh piece of Lillie's stationery. While waiting for food, guests who want to participate can write their own anonymous message for somebody attending a future brunch. There is no obligation to take part.

The new note will be placed back into the envelope and passed on to another customer at a later brunch, while guests can take the message they received home with them.

The owner originally considered creating a communal 'Be Kind Box' from which anybody feeling low could select an anonymous uplifting message. Concerns that an unrestricted box might not always be used in the positive spirit intended led to the more controlled table-envelope idea instead.

The concept is based on a simple recognition that people rarely know what somebody else may be dealing with behind the scenes and that a small act of kindness, including a few thoughtful words from a stranger, can sometimes make a significant difference to someone's day.

Lillie's says the initiative is its own small way of spreading kindness one message at a time, built around the message: 'In a world where you can be anything, be kind.'

The initiative will launch as part of Lillie's Bottomless Brunch offering when the Whitworth venue opens.

Alcohol is for adults aged 18 and over. Please drink responsibly.

articles.title: Prehistoric survivor growing in Syke herb garden has roots stretching back 300 million years
articles.excerpt: Residents picking herbs from a community garden in Syke are being invited to help tackle horsetail — a persistent weed whose ancestors grew locally more than 300 million years ago.
articles.content_html:
A troublesome weed growing in a community herb garden in Syke has a remarkable connection to the landscape's prehistoric past — with its ancestors dating back more than 300 million years.

Residents are being encouraged to help maintain the community herb garden while collecting fresh herbs to take home.

The garden is open for people to pick herbs for their own use, but volunteers are asking visitors who have a few spare minutes to lend a hand with some weeding at the same time.

One plant in particular is proving difficult to control: horsetail, also commonly known as mare's tail.

While modern gardeners may regard it as a persistent nuisance, horsetail belongs to an extraordinarily ancient group of plants whose history stretches back to long before dinosaurs walked the Earth.

During the Carboniferous period, more than 300 million years ago, relatives of today's horsetails grew across the landscapes that would eventually become northern England.

Among them were Calamites — tree-like plants related to modern horsetails which could grow many metres tall and formed part of the vast Carboniferous vegetation.

Evidence of that lost landscape can still be found locally. A fossil discovered in a quarry at Tonacliffe shows the distinctive remains of Calamites, providing a physical connection between the plants growing here hundreds of millions of years ago and the much smaller horsetails residents battle in gardens today.

Carboniferous plant fossils can also be found within rocks across the surrounding moorland, reflecting a period when the area's environment looked dramatically different from the Pennine landscape residents know today.

People remain welcome to collect herbs from the community garden, but anyone visiting is being encouraged to pull a few weeds while they are there.

As the volunteers joked, nobody wants today's horsetail growing to the size of its Carboniferous grandparents.

The community garden is maintained for local people to enjoy, and even a few minutes of weeding can help keep it productive and accessible for everyone.

articles.title: Plans for 45 homes behind Greenvale unanimously deferred after more than 290 objections
articles.excerpt: Councillors have unanimously deferred a planning application for 45 homes on land behind Greenvale in Bamford after campaigners raised concerns over transport, drainage, biodiversity, design and the absence of a wider masterplan.
articles.content_html:
A controversial planning application for 45 homes on land behind Greenvale in Bamford has been unanimously deferred after a packed Planning Committee meeting and more than 290 public objections.

The application had been recommended for approval by planning officers, but strong public interest saw it moved to the first item on the committee agenda.

Claire, chair of Bamford Green Belt Action Group, Dr Barry Lewis and Councillor Steve Anstee addressed the committee, asking councillors either to refuse the proposal or defer a decision while outstanding issues were examined further.

Campaigners raised a wide range of concerns, including the absence of a comprehensive masterplan for the wider allocation of around 450 homes and the lack of an infrastructure phasing and delivery strategy.

Transport was another major issue. Objectors highlighted Transport for Greater Manchester's position that effective transport mitigation could not yet be determined, while concerns were also raised over the proposed access through Greenvale and Norford Way rather than Norden Road.

Existing drainage and pedestrian-safety problems were raised during the meeting. Dr Lewis highlighted drainage issues already experienced on Norford Way and also questioned proposals relating to affordable and social housing beneath power lines.

Environmental concerns included a reported 39 per cent biodiversity net loss, rather than the 10 per cent biodiversity net gain required under current rules. Campaigners also pointed to outstanding concerns from ecology and urban-design officers.

United Utilities was said to have requested an allocation-wide drainage masterplan, while further concerns were raised about design, affordable housing, recreational facilities and the absence of what campaigners considered appropriate pre-application public consultation.

More than 290 objections have been submitted by members of the public.

Following debate, councillors voted unanimously to defer the application until September to allow further work and clarification.

The decision does not amount to a refusal of the proposed development. The application remains live and is expected to return to councillors once the outstanding matters have been considered.

Bamford Green Belt Action Group described the deferral as an important result and thanked residents who attended the meeting, submitted objections or supported the campaign.

Rochdale Daily will report further developments when the application returns to the Planning Committee.

articles.title: Got a Uniform For All order waiting? Balderstone Library needs the shelf space
articles.excerpt: The school uniform reuse scheme says its collection point is 'busier than Amazon's warehouse' - and is asking families with ready-to-collect orders to pick them up to make room for new deliveries.
articles.content_html:
Families with a school uniform order waiting at Balderstone Library are being asked to collect it as soon as possible - because the shelves are full and new deliveries are arriving fast.

Uniform For All, the borough scheme that gives pre-loved school uniform a second life, says anyone who has received an order-ready-to-pick-up email from www.uniformforall.co.uk should call in and collect it promptly to make space. "It's busier than Amazon's warehouse at the Uniform For All office right now," the scheme said.

What is Uniform For All?

Uniform For All collects donated school uniform - the coats, jumpers, polo shirts, trousers and PE kit that children outgrow long before they wear out - checks and sorts it, and passes it on to families across the borough. Orders are placed through the website and collected locally, with Balderstone Library serving as a collection and donation point.

The idea is simple but the impact is real. Kitting a child out for September can cost families well over a hundred pounds per child, and for households already stretched by rent, bills and food, uniform costs land at exactly the wrong time of year. A reuse scheme means good clothing goes to a child who needs it instead of landfill, families keep money in their pockets, and children start term dressed the same as everyone else.

With the summer holidays in full swing and the new school year only weeks away, demand is at its annual peak - hence the plea for prompt collections.

How to donate

If you have school uniform your children have outgrown, you can drop it off at Balderstone Library too. Clean, wearable items are what the scheme needs most. And if your child needs uniform for September, orders can be placed at www.uniformforall.co.uk.
