articles.title: Shoppers donate 368 kilos of food at Rochdale Foodbank's Morrisons Kingsway drive
articles.excerpt: Generous shoppers added extra items to their trolleys over two days at Morrisons Kingsway, donating 368kg of food. How the foodbank works, how to get help - and how to give it.
articles.content_html:
Shoppers at Morrisons Kingsway have donated a remarkable 368 kilos of food to Rochdale Foodbank after a two-day food drive at the store last Thursday and Friday.

The foodbank thanked all the generous shoppers who added extra items to their shopping, saying donations came in all shapes and sizes and included many of its most needed items. The charity also paid special tribute to the volunteers who staffed the collection and made the event a success, adding that every single item received will make a big difference to its clients.

Rochdale Foodbank has been part of life in the town for more than a decade. Registered as a charity in its own right in 2017, it operates as part of the Trussell network of food banks and is run almost entirely by volunteers - around 70 of them - who sort, date-check and pack donated food into emergency parcels at its base off Newgate in the town centre.

How the foodbank works

The foodbank operates on a referral system. Care professionals - including GPs, health visitors, social workers, Citizens Advice staff, welfare officers, the police and probation services - identify people in crisis and issue them with a foodbank voucher. That voucher can then be exchanged at a foodbank session for an emergency parcel containing at least three days of nutritionally balanced food. Volunteers meet clients over a cup of tea and can signpost them to agencies able to help with the longer-term problem, from debt advice to benefits support.

Alongside its main sessions, the foodbank has expanded in recent years. A Saturday morning session runs at Branches Christian Fellowship in Smallbridge, where clients can collect parcels between 10am and 12pm, and the charity has also opened Rochdale Central Pantry in the Rochdale Exchange Shopping Centre - a membership pantry for people who have recently needed foodbank support and could use a little extra help each week.

If you need help, you can call the foodbank on 0300 102 1646 or visit rochdale.foodbank.org.uk, which lists the organisations able to issue vouchers.

How to donate

More than nine in ten items given out by Trussell network food banks are donated by the public, which is why collections like the Morrisons drive matter so much. There are permanent donation points in Rochdale's larger supermarkets, including Tesco, Asda and Morrisons, intended for food purchased in-store. Larger donations can be dropped off at the foodbank's warehouse via the Newgate service area - ring ahead on 0300 102 1646 for big deliveries - and the foodbank publishes a shopping list of the items it most urgently needs on its website. Money donations, which help cover running costs and fill gaps in donated stock, can also be made through the website.

As the foodbank itself puts it: even if it's just one tin every week, every tin helps.

articles.title: Lord-Lieutenant's visit, a surprise inspection passed and a packed cafe: quite a week for Whitworth's Stronger Together
articles.excerpt: The Whitworth carers' group welcomed the King's representative in Lancashire, retained its 5-star hygiene rating in a surprise inspection, and saw its Community Cafe overflow into the main hall — all in one week.
articles.content_html:
A remarkable week for Whitworth carers' group Stronger Together began with a royal representative at the door and ended with a cafe so busy it spilled into the main hall.

On Monday the group welcomed the Lord-Lieutenant of Lancashire, Amanda Parker, and her husband Robert. Mrs Parker is His Majesty The King's personal representative in Lancashire and the first woman to hold the role in the county in almost five hundred years, and her visit is a mark of how far the volunteer-run group has come.

The same day brought a test of a different kind: an unannounced visit from environmental health officers just before lunch service. The inspectors found everything in order and the group retained its food hygiene rating of 5, the top score, which it has held since Rossendale Borough Council first awarded it in December 2024.

By Tuesday the group's Community Cafe was packed, with every table full and half of the main hall pressed into service to seat everyone.

Stronger Together was founded in 2023 by Angela Forster and Kathleen Proctor, both unpaid carers themselves, after they found there was nowhere locally for carers to turn for support. What began as a weekly coffee morning has grown into something much bigger, now based at The Ashcroft on Market Street, where volunteers serve more than 70 fresh, home-cooked meals every week alongside cakes and unlimited drinks, all free of charge with donation pots for those who wish to give.

The group describes itself as a warm, safe space offering advice and emotional and practical support, with activities including prize bingo, crafts and quizzes, and it runs entirely on fundraising, raffles, donations and grants. A crowdfunded project launched last year added gentle exercise sessions with a qualified trainer, healthy eating advice and a singing group open to all ages and abilities.

Recognition has followed. The founders received a Mayor's Special Award at the Whitworth Business and Community Awards in 2023, with the then Mayor of Whitworth describing the pair as truly inspirational to the community. The group went on to win the Not-for-Profit category at the Rossendale Business Awards, and this summer it was shortlisted for Community Group of the Year at the Pride of Rossendale Awards.

Reflecting on the week, the founders thanked the group's volunteers and supporters, saying the group is truly blessed in the people around it.

Anyone who would like to support Stronger Together, volunteer or find out about its sessions can contact the group through its Facebook page.

articles.title: Elderly lady found after incredible community effort
articles.excerpt: A woman in her 70s who went missing in Newhey has been found after hundreds of residents joined Greater Manchester Police in an extraordinary community search.
articles.content_html:
An elderly woman who went missing in Newhey has been found following an extraordinary community effort involving hundreds of local residents.

Christine, who is in her 70s, was reported missing earlier in the evening, prompting an urgent response from Greater Manchester Police and a huge mobilisation across Newhey and the surrounding area.

As concern grew, residents left their homes to help officers search on the ground. People walked streets, paths and open spaces, checked nearby areas and shared information rapidly across community groups in an effort to bring Christine home.

The response was remarkable. Hundreds of people are understood to have assisted either directly with searches or by sharing appeals and helping coordinate information alongside GMP.

At around 11pm, local woman Charlotte Rigby found Christine. In a touching detail after hours of worry, Christine was found clutching a bunch of flowers.

News that she had been located was met with enormous relief across the community, bringing a frightening evening to the best possible conclusion.

Tonight demonstrated Newhey and the wider Rochdale borough at its very best. Residents did not simply share a post and hope for good news. They put on their shoes, went outside and actively helped search for someone who needed them.

Credit must also go to Greater Manchester Police and everyone who supported the search, but special recognition is due to the countless members of the public who gave their time and refused to give up.

The borough should be very proud tonight. This was community spirit in its purest form, and the outcome is the great news everyone had been hoping for.

Out of respect for Christine and her family, no further personal or medical details should be shared unless released through official channels.

articles.title: Heywood singer-songwriter releases heartfelt debut single 'Rewind'
articles.excerpt: Twenty-year-old Heywood singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson has achieved a lifelong ambition with the release of her debut single, Rewind, a soulful pop track inspired by heartbreak, hope and moving forward.
articles.content_html:
A young musician from Heywood has realised a lifelong dream with the release of her debut single.

Twenty-year-old singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson released her first original song, Rewind, on 31 July. The soulful pop track draws on her own experience of heartbreak and the realisation that someone she believed was 'the one' ultimately was not the right person after all.

Music has always played a central role in Rhiannon's life, and releasing her own song is something she says she has dreamed about since childhood.

"Having my own song has always been my biggest dream, so finally releasing Rewind is such an emotional and proud moment for me," she said.

Rhiannon worked alongside her friend, songwriter and producer Jack Carroll, who helped write and produce the track in his studio. She cites Sienna Spiro as one of her biggest musical inspirations.

The response to Rewind has already been overwhelming.

"Seeing people say they love my song means everything to me. I hope when people hear it, they remember there is always a light at the end of the tunnel and that things do get better with time."

Looking ahead, Rhiannon hopes to release an EP and continue sharing her music with the world.

"One of my biggest dreams is to hear my music played on the radio. If people enjoy Rewind, I would be so grateful if they could share it and help more people discover my music."

She added: "Thank you to everyone who has supported me so far. I appreciate every listen, every comment and every share — it truly means the world to me."

Rewind is available now on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. Rhiannon can also be followed on Facebook, Instagram at rhiannon_t05 and TikTok at @rhiannonthompsonxx.

articles.title: Veterans invited to weekly breakfast club as Rochdale continues to support Armed Forces community
articles.excerpt: Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being encouraged to attend a free weekly breakfast club in Heywood, offering friendship, support and an opportunity to reconnect with fellow servicemen and women.
articles.content_html:
Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being invited to attend a weekly Armed Forces Breakfast Club held every Thursday morning at The Flying Horse Hotel in Heywood.

Supported by Rochdale Borough Council, the breakfast club has become a welcoming meeting place for former members of the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force. Breakfast is served between 9am and 10am every Thursday, with organisers reporting that thousands of breakfasts have now been served since the initiative began.

While the event offers a free breakfast, its real purpose is bringing veterans together. Leaving military service can often mean leaving behind the camaraderie and close friendships built over years of service. The breakfast club provides an opportunity to reconnect with fellow veterans, share experiences and offer informal peer support in a relaxed environment.

Rochdale has a proud military heritage stretching back generations. The borough has long been associated with the Lancashire Fusiliers and today remains home to a significant Armed Forces community, including serving personnel, reservists, veterans and military families. Many continue serving their communities long after leaving the military through volunteering, public service and local charities.

Research has consistently shown that social connection can play a vital role in improving wellbeing, particularly among veterans who may experience loneliness or find the transition to civilian life challenging. Community initiatives such as breakfast clubs provide an important opportunity to maintain friendships, reduce isolation and ensure no veteran feels forgotten.

The club is open to any military veteran, regardless of how long they served or when they left the Armed Forces. Whether someone completed a full career or served for only a short period, organisers say everyone who has worn the uniform is welcome.

The Armed Forces Breakfast Club takes place every Thursday between 9am and 10am at The Flying Horse Hotel, Heywood.

Rochdale has always been a borough that values those who have served. While remembrance services rightly honour military sacrifice each November, supporting veterans throughout the year is equally important. Initiatives such as the Heywood Breakfast Club demonstrate how something as simple as sharing breakfast can strengthen friendships, improve wellbeing and remind those who have served that their contribution continues to be appreciated by the community.

articles.title: Late-night fireworks return to Shawclough and Healey as residents' frustration grows
articles.excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey have reported a second consecutive evening of fireworks after 11pm, with growing frustration over disrupted sleep, distressed pets and concerns for wildlife near Healey Dell Nature Reserve.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Shawclough and Healey have once again reported being disturbed by late-night fireworks, with explosions heard at approximately 11.21pm on Sunday evening. The latest incident marks the second consecutive night of reports, leaving many residents questioning when meaningful action will be taken to tackle the ongoing nuisance.

For many households, the issue extends far beyond a brief display. Parents have described children being woken after bedtime, pet owners report anxious and distressed animals, and residents working early shifts say repeated interruptions to their sleep are becoming increasingly difficult to tolerate.

The repeated use of fireworks late at night has also prompted renewed concerns for local wildlife. Healey Dell Nature Reserve, together with the surrounding woodland, provides important habitat for nesting birds, bats and other protected species. Wildlife organisations have long warned that unexpected loud explosions can disturb feeding, nesting and breeding behaviour, particularly during sensitive periods of the year.

Residents have increasingly questioned whether existing legislation is sufficient to prevent repeated anti-social use of fireworks. While fireworks can be legally purchased and used subject to restrictions, businesses selling them must comply with licensing and storage regulations. However, any decision to suspend or revoke a retailer's licence would require evidence that they had breached those legal requirements. Simply because fireworks are being misused by individuals does not automatically mean a retailer has acted unlawfully.

Enforcement remains difficult, particularly when fireworks are discharged from private property under the cover of darkness. Identifying those responsible often relies on witness evidence, CCTV or reports made at the time of the incident.

Nevertheless, residents say patience is wearing thin. After another evening of disrupted sleep, many are calling for stronger enforcement, tighter controls on sales and greater action against those repeatedly using fireworks in residential neighbourhoods late at night.

Fireworks remain an important part of many cultural and community celebrations when used responsibly. However, repeated displays after 11pm in quiet residential areas are a very different matter. Communities should not have to endure nightly disruption, frightened pets, exhausted children and unnecessary disturbance to local wildlife. As complaints continue to mount, many residents are asking a simple question: when will enough finally be enough?

articles.title: Residents raise concerns over anti-social behaviour around Kingsway
articles.excerpt: Residents and businesses are calling for continued action to tackle anti-social behaviour around Kingsway, with police identifying retail crime, ASB and road safety as neighbourhood priorities.
articles.content_html:
Residents and businesses around the Kingsway area of Rochdale are calling for continued action to tackle anti-social behaviour, saying a minority of offenders are affecting what is otherwise one of the borough's busiest retail and employment destinations.

Kingsway has undergone significant regeneration over the past two decades, transforming into a major business and retail hub with national retailers, industrial estates, distribution centres and hundreds of jobs. Thousands of people visit the area every day to shop, work and access nearby facilities.

However, some residents and businesses say issues including nuisance behaviour, shoplifting, groups congregating outside retail premises, dangerous driving and road safety concerns have become increasingly noticeable in recent years.

Greater Manchester Police has identified retail crime at Kingsway Retail Park, anti-social behaviour and road safety as neighbourhood policing priorities for the area. Officers say they have carried out targeted operations against shoplifting, increased patrols and undertaken road traffic enforcement to tackle motorists committing offences.

Police have confirmed that numerous arrests have been made for shoplifting at Morrisons in recent months, while dedicated traffic operations have also been carried out along Kingsway to improve road safety. Regular police surgeries are also being held at Kingsway Retail Park to allow residents and businesses to discuss local concerns directly with neighbourhood officers.

For businesses operating on Kingsway, anti-social behaviour can have a wider economic impact. Retailers say persistent shoplifting, disorder and nuisance behaviour place additional pressure on staff while affecting customer confidence. Many businesses have invested heavily in CCTV, security staff and crime prevention measures, working alongside Greater Manchester Police to identify prolific offenders.

Residents have also highlighted concerns over speeding, dangerous driving and the use of modified vehicles on Kingsway, particularly during evenings. Although the vast majority of motorists use the road responsibly, police say road safety remains one of their key neighbourhood priorities alongside tackling retail crime and anti-social behaviour.

Community safety experts say anti-social behaviour often requires more than enforcement alone. Alongside visible policing, long-term solutions typically involve youth engagement, support for vulnerable individuals, environmental improvements, partnership working with businesses and swift action against repeat offenders.

There have been encouraging signs elsewhere in Rochdale. Greater Manchester Police recently reported significant reductions in anti-social behaviour and wider crime within Rochdale town centre following the introduction of Operation Tetbury, a partnership initiative combining targeted policing with regeneration and community engagement. Officers say anti-social behaviour in the town centre fell by more than 30 per cent during the first year of the operation.

Many residents hope a similarly proactive approach around Kingsway will continue to improve the area, ensuring it remains an attractive destination for shoppers, businesses and investors.

The overwhelming majority of people visiting Kingsway do so without experiencing any problems, and local businesses continue to invest confidently in the area. Nevertheless, residents say continued police visibility, partnership working and prompt action against those responsible for anti-social behaviour will be essential to protecting one of Rochdale's most important commercial centres.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing anti-social behaviour or criminal activity to report it online, by calling 101, or by dialling 999 if there is an immediate risk to life or a crime is in progress.

articles.title: Milnrow author helping children cope with grief through heartfelt storybooks
articles.excerpt: Milnrow author Jane Somers is helping children understand bereavement and pet loss through two beautifully illustrated storybooks, while donating hundreds of copies to hospitals and hospices.
articles.content_html:
A Milnrow author is helping children navigate some of life's most difficult moments through a pair of beautifully illustrated books exploring bereavement and the loss of much-loved pets.

Jane Somers has written two children's books, *Look For The Robin* and *Over Rainbow Bridge*, with the aim of providing comfort, reassurance and hope for young readers experiencing grief.

Drawing on gentle storytelling and colourful illustrations, Jane's books tackle subjects that many families find difficult to discuss, helping children understand loss in an age-appropriate and compassionate way.

Her first book, *Look For The Robin*, tells the story of a friendly robin who reminds grieving children that the special people they have lost are still watching over them and that they continue to be loved. The book has resonated with families, schools and support organisations, with Jane using proceeds from sales to give something back to the community.

Thanks to the support of readers, she has now donated more than 200 copies of the book to hospitals, hospices and other worthy causes, helping children facing bereavement access the story free of charge. Customers ordering directly from her website also receive a handmade robin clay heart trinket as a keepsake.

Jane's second book, *Over Rainbow Bridge*, focuses on another form of grief that is often underestimated – the loss of a family pet. Written in rhyme and accompanied by warm illustrations, the story follows the bond between children and their beloved animals, reassuring young readers that although their pet has crossed Rainbow Bridge, the love and memories they shared remain forever.

The book aims to help parents start conversations about pet loss in a gentle, positive way, recognising that the death of a much-loved animal is often a child's first experience of bereavement. Every copy purchased through Jane's online store includes a complimentary bookmark.

Child psychologists have long recognised the importance of helping children understand grief through honest but reassuring conversations. Books can provide a safe and accessible way for young readers to explore difficult emotions, ask questions and recognise that feelings such as sadness, confusion and loss are a normal part of bereavement.

Jane says her ambition has always been to create stories that offer comfort while giving families practical tools to support children during challenging times. By combining uplifting messages with beautiful illustrations, she hopes her books provide reassurance that love continues even after someone, or a cherished pet, has gone.

Both books retail at £9.99, excluding postage and packaging, and are available directly through Jane's website. As well as supporting an independent local author, every purchase helps her continue donating copies to hospitals, hospices and organisations supporting bereaved children.

Jane's work is another example of the creativity found within Rochdale borough, using the power of storytelling not only to entertain but to make a genuine difference in the lives of local families and children across the country.

articles.title: One man became one walk – now Rochdale's Men Walking and Talking group hopes others will join him
articles.excerpt: A new Men Walking and Talking group has launched in Rochdale, offering men a safe, informal place to meet, walk and talk as organisers hope to tackle loneliness, improve mental wellbeing and reduce the stigma surrounding men's mental health.
articles.content_html:
A simple walk can sometimes be the first step towards changing a life.

That's the message behind Men Walking and Talking, the national Community Interest Company helping men support one another through conversation, companionship and fresh air. The organisation recently launched its Rochdale group, offering a free weekly walk where men can meet without pressure, judgement or the expectation that they have to talk if they don't want to. The walks take place every Thursday evening from Rochdale Cenotaph and are open to all men, with no booking required.

The Rochdale group's organiser recently reflected on one of the challenges facing any new community initiative – sometimes the first person to turn up is the organiser themselves. In recent weeks he has often found himself walking alone, but says he'll continue turning up each Thursday because he believes someone who needs the group will eventually come.

That quiet determination reflects the purpose of Men Walking and Talking. The organisation was founded on the belief that men often find it easier to open up while walking side by side than sitting face-to-face. There is no expectation to share personal struggles, but there is always the opportunity to chat if someone feels ready.

Research has consistently shown that regular physical activity can play an important role in supporting mental wellbeing. Walking outdoors has been linked to reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression, lower stress levels and improved mood. Spending time in nature, exercising regularly and building social connections can all contribute positively to mental health, while loneliness and social isolation are recognised risk factors for poor mental wellbeing.

For many men, however, talking about mental health remains difficult. Although attitudes have improved in recent years, stigma still prevents some people from seeking support. Organisations such as Men Walking and Talking aim to break down those barriers by creating informal spaces where conversation develops naturally rather than feeling like therapy.

The need for initiatives like this remains significant. Suicide continues to be one of the leading causes of death among men under the age of 50 in the UK, with men accounting for around three-quarters of all registered suicides nationally. Behind every statistic are families, friends and communities left dealing with unimaginable loss.

Groups such as Men Walking and Talking cannot replace professional mental health services, but they can provide something equally valuable – connection. A friendly face, a shared walk and the knowledge that someone else understands can make a real difference for people who may otherwise feel isolated.

Community is another important part of the group's mission. Beyond improving physical fitness, regular walks help people build friendships, strengthen local networks and create a sense of belonging. Many participants across the country say they first attended for the walk but kept returning because of the people they met along the way.

The Rochdale organiser hopes more local men will consider giving the group a try. There is no membership, no pressure to speak and no expectation to explain why you've come. Whether someone wants to chat openly, listen quietly or simply enjoy an evening walk with others, they are welcome.

If you are struggling with your mental health, you do not have to face it alone. If you are having thoughts of suicide or feel unable to keep yourself safe, call 999 immediately or go to your nearest Accident and Emergency department. You can also contact Samaritans free of charge on 116 123, email jo@samaritans.org, or reach out to CALM (Campaign Against Living Miserably) on 0800 58 58 58 or through its webchat service. If your situation is not an emergency but you need support, speak to your GP or contact NHS 111 for advice.

Sometimes the hardest part is taking the first step. For one Rochdale volunteer, that first step has meant walking alone while waiting for others to join him. He hopes that, before long, those solitary walks will become conversations shared with men who simply needed someone to walk beside.

articles.title: Record month for The Strand Community Café as community support continues to grow
articles.excerpt: The Strand Community Café has celebrated its busiest month ever, introducing new outdoor seating, a book swap, a £1.50 children's menu and a family duck-hunting competition while thanking the community for its continued support.
articles.content_html:
The Strand Community Café in Kirkholt is celebrating its busiest month since opening, with volunteers thanking customers, supporters and local organisations for helping the community venue continue to grow.

The café says the past month has been its most successful to date, with increasing numbers of local residents visiting for breakfast, lunch, daily specials and community activities. Managers say the continued support from customers has allowed them to introduce new initiatives while expanding what the café can offer local people.

One of the highlights of the month was the café's World Cup Competition, organised in partnership with its sister venue, The Hive at the Million Pavilion. Together, the two cafés distributed 60 back-to-school packs to local children, helping families prepare for the new school year.

The café has also invested in additional outdoor seating, providing more space for visitors to enjoy refreshments during the warmer months. A newly introduced Book Swap Club has quickly become a popular feature, encouraging visitors to bring along books they have finished and exchange them for something new to read.

Food continues to be at the heart of the café's success. Daily specials have proved particularly popular with regular customers, while the café says its freshly prepared bacon sandwiches remain one of its biggest sellers, with demand showing no signs of slowing.

With the summer holidays now underway, The Strand Community Café has also introduced a £1.50 children's menu in a bid to provide affordable meals for local families during the school break. The initiative forms part of the café's wider commitment to ensuring the venue remains accessible to everyone in the community.

Perhaps the most unusual attraction currently drawing visitors through the doors is the café's new 'How Many Ducks?' competition. Dozens of small rubber ducks have been hidden in plain sight throughout the café, challenging customers of all ages to see how many they can spot during their visit.

The light-hearted competition has quickly become a talking point among visitors, particularly younger customers, adding another family-friendly activity alongside the café's food and community events.

In a message thanking supporters, the team said the café's success would not have been possible without the continued backing of its loyal customers, volunteers and partners. Special thanks were given to Rochdale Boroughwide Housing for placing its trust in HMR Circle – The Volunteer Drivers Service to manage the café, alongside the community hall and kitchen facilities at The Strand in Kirkholt.

The café has become more than simply a place to eat, evolving into an important community hub where residents can meet friends, enjoy affordable meals and take part in local activities. Initiatives such as the Book Swap Club, children's competitions and low-cost family meals reflect its growing role in supporting the wider Kirkholt community.

With record visitor numbers, expanding facilities and a busy programme of community initiatives, The Strand Community Café says it is looking forward to building on its success throughout the rest of the year. In the meantime, anyone visiting is being encouraged to enjoy a bite to eat, browse the books and see just how many hidden rubber ducks they can find.

articles.title: Hundreds enjoy sunshine, music and family fun at Springhill Hospice Summer Garden Celebration
articles.excerpt: Families, supporters and volunteers gathered at Springhill Hospice for its annual Summer Garden Celebration, enjoying live music, games, food and award-winning gardens while raising vital funds for hospice care.
articles.content_html:
Springhill Hospice welcomed families, supporters and members of the local community to its annual Summer Garden Celebration on Sunday, with visitors enjoying an afternoon of live entertainment, garden games, artisan stalls and fundraising in the Hospice's award-winning grounds.

Running from 11am until 3pm, the free family-friendly event once again opened the Hospice's gardens to the public, giving visitors the opportunity to explore the landscaped grounds while supporting one of Rochdale's best-loved charities. Adult visitors were invited to make a suggested £2 donation, with proceeds helping to fund the specialist palliative and end-of-life care provided by Springhill Hospice.

Throughout the day, the Hospice grounds were filled with families enjoying live music, children's entertainment, traditional garden games and a wide variety of food, drink and shopping stalls. Local traders offered seasonal produce, decorative gifts and artisan products, while visitors relaxed in the sunshine and explored the colourful gardens maintained by the Hospice's gardening team.

The Summer Garden Celebration has become one of Springhill Hospice's most popular community fundraising events, combining a relaxed family day out with an opportunity for residents to learn more about the Hospice's work and the services it provides to patients and families across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton and the surrounding areas.

Many visitors took the opportunity to browse the Hospice's gardens, which have received national recognition in recent years for their design and maintenance. The gardens provide an important therapeutic environment for patients and families throughout the year, offering peaceful outdoor spaces where people can spend time together during difficult periods in their lives.

Volunteers, staff and supporters were on hand throughout the afternoon to welcome guests, assist with activities and help raise vital funds. Events such as the Summer Garden Celebration play an important role in supporting the Hospice, which relies heavily on charitable donations and community fundraising to continue providing its specialist care free of charge.

The event attracted families of all ages, with children enjoying games and entertainment while adults explored the various stalls and food outlets. Live music throughout the afternoon helped create a relaxed festival atmosphere as visitors gathered across the Hospice grounds.

Ahead of the event, organisers had promised 'a spectacular day' featuring garden games, live music and delicious food, and Sunday's celebration appeared to deliver exactly that as supporters turned out to enjoy the Hospice's annual summer gathering.

Springhill Hospice provides specialist palliative and end-of-life care for people living with life-limiting illnesses across Rochdale and the surrounding boroughs. As an independent charity, it receives only part of its funding from the NHS, with the majority raised through donations, fundraising events, retail income and the ongoing support of the local community.

The success of events such as the Summer Garden Celebration reflects the strong connection between the Hospice and the communities it serves. Every donation, purchase and ticket helps ensure that patients and their families continue to receive compassionate care and support when they need it most.

With another successful Summer Garden Celebration complete, attention now turns to Springhill Hospice's busy calendar of fundraising events over the coming months, as the charity continues its efforts to raise the funds needed to sustain its vital services for local people.

articles.title: Residents in Shawclough and Healey call for action over late-night fireworks
articles.excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey are calling for stronger action after repeated late-night fireworks disrupted neighbourhoods, with concerns over sleep, vulnerable people, wildlife and the difficulty of identifying those responsible.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Shawclough and Healey are calling for stronger action after repeated late-night fireworks disturbed neighbourhoods, with many saying explosions after 11pm are affecting sleep, frightening children and causing distress to vulnerable people. While organised displays remain an important part of celebrations throughout the year, many residents say fireworks are increasingly being let off on ordinary evenings with little regard for those living nearby.

The latest complaints prompted a strong response on social media. Local resident Nick Simpson wrote: "Absolutely outrageous. These people need to be locked up and fined," reflecting frustration shared by others who say the disturbances have become an unwelcome feature of late evenings.

Councillor Shah Wazir also urged residents to report incidents wherever possible. Responding to complaints, he said: "Please report this to police and if you know the address then it will certainly help. Firework at night is totally unacceptable, no matter what occasion."

Fireworks are already regulated by law. In most circumstances they cannot legally be set off between 11pm and 7am, with later cut-off times applying only on Bonfire Night, New Year's Eve, Diwali and Chinese New Year. Retailers can only sell fireworks all year if they hold the appropriate licence, while most other retailers are restricted to seasonal sales.

Despite those laws, many residents believe enforcement remains one of the biggest challenges. Fireworks are usually set off after dark from private gardens, alleyways or open spaces, making it difficult for neighbours to identify exactly where they have come from. By the time officers could arrive, the noise has often stopped and those responsible may have left the area.

Many people are also understandably reluctant to confront those responsible themselves. Approaching unknown individuals late at night carries obvious risks, particularly where alcohol or antisocial behaviour may already be involved. Residents say they often feel they have little practical option beyond reporting incidents after they have happened, despite recognising that successful enforcement depends on accurate information.

The disruption extends far beyond a few loud bangs. Parents describe young children being startled awake and struggling to settle again, while elderly residents and people recovering from illness can lose valuable sleep. Mental health charities have also highlighted the impact unexpected fireworks can have on people living with anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder and other conditions where sudden loud noises may trigger distress.

Wildlife is also affected. Conservation organisations have warned that repeated fireworks can disturb nesting birds and protected species such as bats, while many pet owners report dogs, cats and other animals becoming frightened by sudden explosions. Unlike organised displays, fireworks used without warning leave residents with little opportunity to prepare vulnerable family members or animals.

The issue has prompted wider debate over whether existing laws go far enough or whether stronger enforcement is needed. While legislation already restricts when fireworks can be used, many residents argue the difficulty lies in identifying those responsible quickly enough for police to take effective action.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing the illegal use of fireworks or persistent antisocial behaviour to report it, particularly where an address or precise location can be provided. As concerns continue to emerge from Shawclough, Healey and other parts of the borough, many residents hope greater awareness, responsible use and more effective enforcement will help restore quieter evenings to Rochdale's neighbourhoods.

articles.title: Veterans charity says demand for support is growing after emotional day for volunteers
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale organisation supporting military veterans and disadvantaged young people has issued an emotional appeal for greater support after a recent case reminded volunteers why their work remains so important.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale-based community organisation supporting military veterans and disadvantaged young people has issued an emotional appeal for greater public support after what it described as one of the most challenging days in its history.

Get Together After Serving CIC (GTAS) said a recent case involving people it was assisting left members of its leadership team deeply affected, highlighting the growing pressures facing both former servicemen and women and vulnerable children within the community. While the organisation has not released details of the case in order to protect those involved, it says the experience reinforced the urgent need for the support services it provides every day.

In a heartfelt statement shared with supporters, GTAS explained that one of its directors, Wayne, was left visibly emotional after witnessing the circumstances surrounding the latest referral. According to the organisation, despite a lifetime of experience dealing with trauma, military service and personal hardship, the situation served as a powerful reminder that many people continue to struggle in silence.

The organisation says these moments rarely become public. Instead, staff and volunteers often work quietly behind the scenes, providing practical assistance, emotional support and signposting to those who find themselves in crisis. GTAS says much of its work takes place away from social media and public attention, with the focus remaining firmly on helping individuals rather than seeking recognition.

Founded to support former members of the Armed Forces while also creating opportunities for disadvantaged children and young people, Get Together After Serving CIC has steadily expanded its role within the local community. Alongside offering companionship and welfare support for veterans, the organisation works to reduce social isolation, improve wellbeing and create positive opportunities for young people who may otherwise feel overlooked.

Veterans' charities across the UK have repeatedly highlighted the complex challenges many former service personnel face after leaving the Armed Forces. Although the transition to civilian life is smooth for many, others experience difficulties relating to housing, employment, mental health, financial hardship or adjusting to life outside military service. Community organisations often play an important role by offering early intervention before problems escalate.

At the same time, many charities supporting children and young people have reported increasing demand for services as families continue to face financial pressures and wider social challenges. Community groups such as GTAS frequently rely on volunteers, donations and fundraising to continue delivering projects that might otherwise be unavailable to those who need them.

GTAS says its work demonstrates how relatively small organisations can have a significant impact despite operating with limited resources. Its latest appeal emphasises that a dedicated team of volunteers continues to provide support every day because they believe nobody should have to face hardship alone.

In its statement, the organisation said the latest events reinforced its belief that its work is not simply beneficial but, in some cases, life-changing. It described helping veterans find safety and dignity while giving disadvantaged young people opportunities, stability and a place where they feel valued.

The charity is now encouraging local residents, businesses and community organisations to become involved, whether by volunteering, making donations, fundraising or simply helping raise awareness of its work. It believes that increasing community support will allow it to reach more people before problems become crises.

Like many community interest companies, GTAS operates in an increasingly challenging funding environment. Demand for grassroots support services has grown while competition for grants and charitable funding has become more intense. As a result, many organisations rely heavily on local goodwill to sustain their work.

The latest appeal serves as a reminder that behind every public fundraising campaign or social media post are real people facing difficult circumstances, often away from public view. For the volunteers involved, success is not measured by headlines or recognition but by the number of people who receive help when they need it most.

Anyone wishing to learn more about Get Together After Serving CIC, volunteer their time or support its work can find further information through the organisation's social media channels. GTAS says every contribution, no matter how small, helps strengthen its ability to support veterans and young people across the Rochdale area.
